In coordinates for a Riemannian metric with matrix $(g_{ij})$ and inverse $(g^{ij})$, its Levi–Civita symbols are
$$\Gamma^k{}_{ij}=\tfrac12\sum_\ell g^{k\ell}(\partial_i g_{j\ell}+\partial_j g_{i\ell}-\partial_\ell g_{ij}).$$

For an affine connection as in [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]] and coordinates $(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, its **Christoffel symbols** in this chart are the unique smooth functions $\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ such that
$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k.$$
The first lower index $i$ is the differentiating direction and the second lower index $j$ labels the differentiated vector field. In the coordinate frame, the one-forms from [[def-connection-one-form-in-a-local-frame]] are $\omega^k{}_j=\sum_i\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\,dx^i$. A different chart generally has different symbols. This definition asserts neither symmetry in $i,j$ nor tensorial transformation.

For dimension one there is one smooth coefficient $\Gamma^1{}_{11}$; in dimension zero there are no coefficients. All statements are local, and at a boundary chart the derivatives are the smooth up-to-boundary coordinate derivatives.

An **affine connection** on a smooth manifold $M$ is a connection on the tangent bundle $TM$ in the sense of [[def-connection-on-a-smooth-vector-bundle]]. Thus it assigns a vector field $
abla_XY$ to two vector fields and is function-linear in the differentiating direction $X$, real-linear in $Y$, and obeys $
abla_X(fY)=X(f)Y+f
abla_XY$.

The word affine imposes neither a metric nor torsion freeness. The tangent-bundle specialization allows the Lie bracket of $X,Y$ to be compared with their covariant derivatives; there is no corresponding bracket on sections of a general vector bundle. Manifolds with boundary are allowed, and tangent vectors at their boundary need not be tangent to the boundary. The empty and zero-dimensional manifolds have the unique tangent-bundle connection.
If $(U,x)$ is a smooth chart on an $n$-manifold $M$ with $p\in U$, then the coordinate derivations $\partial_1|_p,\dots,\partial_n|_p$ form a basis of $T_pM$.

Let $(U,x)$ be a smooth chart on an $n$-manifold $M$, and let $X$ be a vector
field on $U$. Then $X$ is smooth if and only if there exist smooth functions
$X^1,\dots,X^n:U\to\mathbb R$ such that

$$ X=\sum_{i=1}^n X^i \frac{\partial}{\partial x^i} $$

on $U$.

In a coordinate chart, use the convention

$$\nabla_{\partial_i}\partial_k=\Gamma^\ell{}_{ik}\partial_\ell,\qquad R(\partial_i,\partial_j)\partial_k=R^\ell{}_{kij}\partial_\ell.$$

Then

$$R^\ell{}_{kij}=\partial_i\Gamma^\ell{}_{jk}-\partial_j\Gamma^\ell{}_{ik}+\Gamma^m{}_{jk}\Gamma^\ell{}_{im}-\Gamma^m{}_{ik}\Gamma^\ell{}_{jm}.$$

Let $\nabla$ be an affine connection on a smooth manifold $M$. For $p\in M$
and $u,v,w\in T_pM$, choose smooth local extensions $X,Y,Z$ and set

$$R_p(u,v)w:=(R(X,Y)Z)_p.$$

This is independent of the extensions, is trilinear in $(u,v,w)$, and varies
smoothly with $p$. Equivalently,

$$\mathcal R_p(\alpha,u,v,w):=\alpha\bigl(R_p(u,v)w\bigr)$$

is a smooth type $(1,3)$ tensor field. We use $R$ for both this tensor and its
vector-valued representative.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, let $\nabla$ be its unique
Levi–Civita connection, and let $R$ be the curvature tensor with the sign fixed
above. The **Riemann curvature four-tensor** is the covariant tensor

$$\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W):=g(R(X,Y)Z,W).$$

Thus the first two arguments are the two differentiating slots, the third is
the field acted on, and the fourth lowers the output index. In coordinates,
if $R(\partial_i,\partial_j)\partial_k=R^m{}_{kij}\partial_m$, then
$R_{ijkl}=g_{lm}R^m{}_{kij}$ under this argument order. This convention makes
$\operatorname{Rm}(u,v,v,u)$ positive on a positively curved round sphere.

The definition uses no chosen frame. On an empty or zero-dimensional manifold
it gives the unique zero four-tensor; in dimension one the same formula applies
and later symmetries force it to vanish. It is valid up to the boundary when a
Riemannian manifold with boundary is supplied.

For $X,Y\in T_pM$, the **Ricci curvature** is

$$\operatorname{Ric}_p(X,Y):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(Z\longmapsto R_p(Z,X)Y\bigr).$$

The trace is the basis-independent trace of this endomorphism of $T_pM$; no
orthonormal basis is part of the definition. Equivalently, Ricci contracts the
first input of the curvature endomorphism with its output. The next lemma
proves smoothness and symmetry and derives the orthonormal-basis formula.

On a zero-dimensional tangent space the endomorphism and its empty trace are
zero. On an empty manifold this is the unique empty two-tensor, and the same
pointwise definition applies in dimension one and at a boundary point. No
choice of bases over the points of $M$ is made.

This item assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, namely [[def-countable-choice|countable choice]]. In the propagated dependency chain, that assumption is required through [[lem-ricci-curvature-is-symmetric-and-basis-independent]]; after those interfaces are fixed, the remaining local or finite argument makes no additional countable-family choice.

Use the inverse metric to raise the first covariant index of
$\operatorname{Ric}$, obtaining the endomorphism
$\operatorname{Ric}^{\sharp}:T_pM\to T_pM$ characterized by

$$g_p(\operatorname{Ric}^{\sharp}X,Y)=\operatorname{Ric}_p(X,Y).$$

The **scalar curvature** is the smooth function

$$S(p):=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Ric}^{\sharp}_p)=\operatorname{tr}_g\operatorname{Ric}_p.$$

The musical isomorphism makes $\operatorname{Ric}^{\sharp}$ well-defined and
smooth, and tensor contraction makes its trace intrinsic. In any orthonormal
basis $(e_1,\ldots,e_n)$ of $T_pM$, the metric dual basis is
$(g_p(e_i,\mathord\cdot))$, so

$$S(p)=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Ric}_p(e_i,e_i).$$

Thus the displayed sum is independent of the orthonormal basis. In dimension
zero it is the empty sum $0$; on an empty manifold it is the unique empty
smooth function. The definition is unchanged in dimension one or at boundary
points. Positive definiteness excludes a degenerate metric, and fixing a
single finite basis at an arbitrary point requires no global choice.

This item assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, namely [[def-countable-choice|countable choice]]. In the propagated dependency chain, that assumption is required through [[thm-algebraic-symmetries-of-the-riemann-tensor]]; after those interfaces are fixed, the remaining local or finite argument makes no additional countable-family choice.

Let $\sigma\subseteq T_pM$ be a two-dimensional linear subspace and let
$(X,Y)$ be any ordered basis of $\sigma$. Its **sectional curvature** is

$$K(\sigma):=\frac{\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Y,X)}{g(X,X)g(Y,Y)-g(X,Y)^2}.$$

The denominator is the Gram determinant of the independent pair $(X,Y)$ and
is strictly positive because $g$ is positive definite. The next lemma proves
that the quotient is unchanged by the chosen ordered basis. With the sign
convention fixed above, an orthonormal tangent two-plane in the unit round
sphere has sectional curvature $+1$.

There are no tangent two-planes in dimensions zero or one, so the definition
has empty domain there rather than assigning a spurious value. No plane exists
on an empty manifold either. The same fibrewise definition applies at a
boundary point.

derivations.claim: (Symbols of the rescaled metric.) In a chart, the matrix of $\gamma_\lambda$ is $\lambda(\gamma_{ij})$ with inverse $\lambda^{-1}(\gamma^{ij})$, and its coordinate derivatives are $\partial_i(\lambda\gamma_{j\ell})=\lambda\,\partial_i\gamma_{j\ell}$. Substituting into [L1], $\Gamma_\lambda{}^k{}_{ij}=\tfrac12\lambda^{-1}\gamma^{k\ell}\lambda(\partial_i\gamma_{j\ell}+\partial_j\gamma_{i\ell}-\partial_\ell\gamma_{ij})=\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$: the symbols of $\gamma_\lambda$ and $\gamma$ agree in every chart.

(Connection equality.) Fix a chart. By [L2] a vector field on its domain is $\sum_if^i\partial_i$ with smooth $f^i$, and the symbols describe the connection on coordinate fields, $
abla_{\partial_i}\partial_j=\sum_k\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k$. Since $
abla$ is function-linear in its first argument and satisfies the Leibniz rule in its second, $
abla_XY=X^a\partial_a(Y^b)\partial_b+X^aY^b
abla_{\partial_a}\partial_b$ for smooth fields; hence two affine connections with the same symbols in every chart agree on all smooth vector fields. By step 1.1 the Levi-Civita connections of $\gamma_\lambda$ and $\gamma$ have the same symbols in every chart, so they are equal.

(Curvature operator equality.) The curvature operator is defined from the connection alone by $R(X,Y)Z=
abla_X
abla_YZ-
abla_Y
abla_XZ-
abla_{[X,Y]}Z$; substituting the common connection of step 2.1 gives $R_\lambda=R$ on smooth fields. Equivalently, the coordinate formula [L3] expresses the components through the common symbols and their derivatives, so the components agree in every chart and [L3] makes the operators equal as $(1,3)$-tensors.

(Ricci equality.) By the definition recalled in [L4], $\operatorname{Ric}(X,Y)$ is the trace of the endomorphism $Z\mapsto R(Z,X)Y$ of $T_p\Sigma$; this trace is computed from the curvature endomorphism and the vector-space structure alone and uses no metric. Since $R_\lambda=R$ by step 3.1, the endomorphisms coincide at every point and so do their traces: $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma_\lambda)=\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)$. In particular no factor of $\lambda$ appears.

(Lowered curvature, scalar curvature and sectional curvature.) At a point, $\operatorname{Rm}_{\gamma_\lambda}(X,Y,Z,W)=(\lambda\gamma)(R_\lambda(X,Y)Z,W)=\lambda\,\gamma(R(X,Y)Z,W)=\lambda\operatorname{Rm}_\gamma(X,Y,Z,W)$ by [L4], step 3.1 and bilinearity of $\gamma$. Taking the metric trace of step 4.1, $S(\gamma_\lambda)=\sum_{i,j}(\lambda\gamma)^{ij}\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma_\lambda)_{ij}=\lambda^{-1}\sum_{i,j}\gamma^{ij}\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)_{ij}=\lambda^{-1}S(\gamma)$, since the inverse metric of $\lambda\gamma$ is $\lambda^{-1}\gamma^{-1}$. Finally, for an independent pair $(u,v)$ the numerator of the sectional curvature of $\gamma_\lambda$ is $\operatorname{Rm}_{\gamma_\lambda}(u,v,v,u)=\lambda\operatorname{Rm}_\gamma(u,v,v,u)$ while the Gram determinant of $(u,v)$ with respect to $\gamma_\lambda$ is $\lambda^2$ times the Gram determinant with respect to $\gamma$; the ratio is therefore multiplied by $\lambda^{-1}$, $K_{\gamma_\lambda}(\sigma)=\lambda^{-1}K_\gamma(\sigma)$. This proves the four claims.

boundaries.reason: The statement is an identity of tensor fields on a smooth manifold and the proof works in an arbitrary chart; no empty family, empty index set or empty interval is quantified, and the two tensor fields in each display are everywhere defined because λ > 0 keeps γ_λ a Riemannian metric.

boundaries.evidence: statement: the hypothesis is λ > 0, so the rescaling is invertible and step 1.1 divides by λ through λ^{-1}γ^{ij}; the excluded zero rescaling would be a degenerate form, not the metric studied here.
step 1.1: substituting λ = 1 returns exactly the symbols of γ, so the lemma reduces to the identity in the trivial rescaling case.

boundaries.reason: The metric γ is Riemannian by hypothesis and λ > 0, so λγ is positive definite as well; no degenerate or indefinite case arises and the statement has nothing to say about one.
The claims are pointwise identities at each point of the boundaryless manifold Σ; no interval, sequence index or limit point is used, so endpoint cases do not arise.

boundaries.evidence: statement and step 2.1: the proof uses one arbitrary chart and the coordinate basis in it, selecting no family of points, charts or bases; the inherited AC_ω is only that of the cited Riemannian suppliers.

boundaries.reason: The lemma asserts a list of equalities, not an equivalence, so there is no forward implication to check separately.
The lemma asserts a list of equalities, not an equivalence, so there is no reverse implication to check separately.

Constant positive lambda cancels in the connection, preserves the (1,3) curvature and covariant Ricci, scales the lowered tensor by lambda and both scalar and sectional curvature by lambda inverse. Gram determinants are positive for independent pairs; zero/one dimensional sectional domains are empty. Inherited countable choice is explicit; no further choice occurs. No defect, no carrier edit.

This item assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, namely [[def-countable-choice|countable choice]]. In the propagated dependency chain, that assumption is required through [[def-constant-sectional-curvature-and-space-form]]; the tensor-determination argument is choice-free.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as inherited through
[[def-constant-sectional-curvature-and-space-form]]; the algebraic proof below
uses no additional choice. A Riemannian manifold has constant sectional
curvature $K$ if and only if

$$R(X,Y)Z=K\bigl(g(Y,Z)X-g(X,Z)Y\bigr).$$

Equivalently,

$$\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W)=K\bigl(g(Y,Z)g(X,W)-g(X,Z)g(Y,W)\bigr).$$

This item assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, namely [[def-countable-choice|countable choice]]. In the propagated dependency chain, that assumption is required through [[def-sectional-curvature]]; after those interfaces are fixed, the remaining local or finite argument makes no additional countable-family choice.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ exactly as in
[[def-geodesically-complete-riemannian-manifold]]. It is used here only through
that supplier's construction of the unique maximal geodesic domains needed to
interpret completeness; the constant-curvature predicate itself makes no further family choice beyond the stated inherited assumption.

A Riemannian manifold has **constant sectional curvature $K\in\mathbb R$**
when every tangent two-plane at every point has sectional curvature $K$. A
connected, boundaryless, geodesically complete Riemannian manifold of constant
sectional curvature is called a **space form** on this page.

This global condition is stronger than saying that, at each point $p$, all
two-planes have some common value $K(p)$; Schur's lemma later proves constancy
of that pointwise value in connected dimension at least three. In dimensions
zero and one there are no tangent two-planes, so the predicate “has constant
sectional curvature $K$” is vacuous for every $K$ and does not determine a
distinguished number. Under the library convention that the empty space is
connected, the empty boundaryless complete manifold is correspondingly a
vacuous space form. These low-dimensional conventions do not affect later
formulas, whose alternating metric model vanishes in dimensions below two.

For $X,Y\in T_pM$, the **Ricci curvature** is

$$\operatorname{Ric}_p(X,Y):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(Z\longmapsto R_p(Z,X)Y\bigr).$$

The trace is the basis-independent trace of this endomorphism of $T_pM$; no
orthonormal basis is part of the definition. Equivalently, Ricci contracts the
first input of the curvature endomorphism with its output. The next lemma
proves smoothness and symmetry and derives the orthonormal-basis formula.

On a zero-dimensional tangent space the endomorphism and its empty trace are
zero. On an empty manifold this is the unique empty two-tensor, and the same
pointwise definition applies in dimension one and at a boundary point. No
choice of bases over the points of $M$ is made.

Ricci curvature is a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor. For every
orthonormal basis $(e_1,\ldots,e_n)$ of $T_pM$,

$$\operatorname{Ric}_p(X,Y)=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Rm}_p(e_i,X,Y,e_i),$$

and the value is independent of the basis.

$\operatorname{Ric}$, obtaining the endomorphism
$\operatorname{Ric}^{\sharp}:T_pM\to T_pM$ characterized by

$$g_p(\operatorname{Ric}^{\sharp}X,Y)=\operatorname{Ric}_p(X,Y).$$

The **scalar curvature** is the smooth function

$$S(p):=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Ric}^{\sharp}_p)=\operatorname{tr}_g\operatorname{Ric}_p.$$

The musical isomorphism makes $\operatorname{Ric}^{\sharp}$ well-defined and
smooth, and tensor contraction makes its trace intrinsic. In any orthonormal
basis $(e_1,\ldots,e_n)$ of $T_pM$, the metric dual basis is

Thus the displayed sum is independent of the orthonormal basis. In dimension
zero it is the empty sum $0$; on an empty manifold it is the unique empty
smooth function. The definition is unchanged in dimension one or at boundary
points. Positive definiteness excludes a degenerate metric, and fixing a
single finite basis at an arbitrary point requires no global choice.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, let $\nabla$ be its unique
Levi–Civita connection, and let $R$ be the curvature tensor with the sign fixed
above. The **Riemann curvature four-tensor** is the covariant tensor

$$\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W):=g(R(X,Y)Z,W).$$

Thus the first two arguments are the two differentiating slots, the third is
the field acted on, and the fourth lowers the output index. In coordinates,
if $R(\partial_i,\partial_j)\partial_k=R^m{}_{kij}\partial_m$, then
$R_{ijkl}=g_{lm}R^m{}_{kij}$ under this argument order. This convention makes
$\operatorname{Rm}(u,v,v,u)$ positive on a positively curved round sphere.

The definition uses no chosen frame. On an empty or zero-dimensional manifold

In the propagated dependency chain, that assumption is required through [[def-scalar-curvature]]; after those interfaces are fixed, the remaining local or finite argument makes no additional countable-family choice.

For symmetric covariant two-tensors $h$ and $k$, their
**Kulkarni–Nomizu product** is the covariant four-tensor

$$\begin{aligned}(h\odot k)(X,Y,Z,T)={}&h(X,T)k(Y,Z)+h(Y,Z)k(X,T)\\&-h(X,Z)k(Y,T)-h(Y,T)k(X,Z).\end{aligned}$$

This fixes the order and sign convention used below. In particular,

$$(g\odot g)(X,Y,Z,T)=2\bigl(g(X,T)g(Y,Z)-g(X,Z)g(Y,T)\bigr),$$

so the constant-sectional-curvature-$K$ tensor is
$(K/2)(g\odot g)$.

On an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with $n\geq 1$, define the
**trace-free Ricci tensor** by

$$\operatorname{Ric}_0:=\operatorname{Ric}-\frac{S}{n}g.$$

Indeed $\operatorname{tr}_g\operatorname{Ric}_0=S-(S/n)n=0$. In dimension
zero, where division by $n$ has no meaning, set $\operatorname{Ric}_0=0$;
this is the unique covariant two-tensor on every zero-dimensional tangent
space.

For $n\geq3$, define the **Weyl curvature tensor** by

$$W:=\operatorname{Rm}-\frac{1}{n-2}(\operatorname{Ric}_0\odot g)-\frac{S}{2n(n-1)}(g\odot g).$$

The next proposition proves that this is an algebraic curvature tensor with
vanishing Ricci contraction and that it is the unique trace-free summand in
the Ricci decomposition. Weyl curvature is not defined by this formula in
dimensions zero, one, or two; the separate low-dimensional curvature formulas
are also proved there.

All constructions are pointwise tensor operations on smooth tensors and so
are smooth, including at boundary points. On an empty manifold of an allowed
fixed dimension they give the corresponding unique empty tensor fields. No
basis is chosen, and the finite contractions make no further family choice beyond the stated inherited assumption. Metric degeneracy is
excluded by the Riemannian hypothesis.

This item assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, namely [[def-countable-choice|countable choice]]. In the propagated dependency chain, that assumption is required through [[def-kulkarni-nomizu-product-trace-free-ricci-and-weyl-curvature]], [[thm-algebraic-symmetries-of-the-riemann-tensor]], [[lem-ricci-curvature-is-symmetric-and-basis-independent]], and [[def-scalar-curvature]]; after those interfaces are fixed, the remaining local or finite argument makes no additional countable-family choice.

On an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with $n\geq3$,

$$\operatorname{Rm}=W+\frac{1}{n-2}(\operatorname{Ric}_0\odot g)+\frac{S}{2n(n-1)}(g\odot g),$$

where $W$ has zero Ricci contraction. This decomposition into a trace-free
curvature tensor, a trace-free-Ricci summand, and a scalar summand is unique.
In dimension three, $W=0$. Separately, in dimension two,

$$\operatorname{Rm}=\frac{S}{4}(g\odot g).$$

derivations.claim: (Clause (a) implies clause (c).) If every tangent two-plane has sectional curvature $k$, then [L1] gives $R(X,Y)Z=k(\gamma(Y,Z)X-\gamma(X,Z)Y)$ at every point of $\Sigma$, which is exactly clause (c); conversely clause (c) is the tensor identity of [L1] from which the sectional curvature $k$ of every two-plane is read off.

(Clause (c) implies clause (b), and $S=6k$ whenever clause (b) holds.) Assume clause (c) and fix $p\in\Sigma$. Choose a $\gamma_p$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $T_p\Sigma$, which exists by [L2]. Substituting [L1] into the trace formula of [L2] gives $\operatorname{Ric}(X,Y)=\sum_{i=1}^3k(\gamma(X,Y)\gamma(e_i,e_i)-\gamma(e_i,Y)\gamma(X,e_i))=k(3\gamma(X,Y)-\gamma(X,Y))=2k\gamma(X,Y)$ for all $X,Y\in T_p\Sigma$, using $\gamma(e_i,e_i)=1$ and $\sum_i\gamma(e_i,Y)\gamma(X,e_i)=\gamma(X,Y)$; this is clause (b). Conversely, under clause (b) the metric trace gives $S=\sum_{i,j}\gamma^{ij}\operatorname{Ric}_{ij}=2k\sum_{i,j}\gamma^{ij}\gamma_{ij}=6k$ and $\operatorname{Ric}_0=\operatorname{Ric}-\tfrac13S\gamma=2k\gamma-2k\gamma=0$ by [L4].

(Clause (b) implies clause (a).) Assume clause (b). By step 2.1, $S=6k$ and $\operatorname{Ric}_0=0$; since the dimension is three, [L4] gives $\operatorname{Rm}=\tfrac{6k}{12}(\gamma\odot\gamma)=\tfrac{k}{2}(\gamma\odot\gamma)$, and [L4] identifies $\tfrac{k}{2}(\gamma\odot\gamma)$ as the constant-sectional-curvature-$k$ tensor, that is, $\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W)=k(\gamma(Y,Z)\gamma(X,W)-\gamma(X,Z)\gamma(Y,W))$; by the definition [L3] of the Riemann four-tensor this reads $R(X,Y)Z=k(\gamma(Y,Z)X-\gamma(X,Z)Y)$, which is clause (c). By the equivalence recalled in [L1], clause (c) is clause (a).

(Conclusion.) Step 1.1 gives (a)$\Rightarrow$(c), step 2.1 gives (c)$\Rightarrow$(b), and step 3.1 gives (b)$\Rightarrow$(a); hence the three clauses are equivalent. The scalar identity $S=6k$ and the vanishing of $\operatorname{Ric}_0$ were proved in step 2.1 under the equivalent hypotheses. No step assumes a value of $k$ beyond $k\in\mathbb R$, and the empty and low-dimensional cases do not arise because $\Sigma$ is a three-manifold.

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]), with smooth atlas
$\mathcal A$ and maximal smooth atlas $[\mathcal A]$
([[def-smooth-atlas]], [[def-smoothly-compatible-charts]]). For $p\in M$ the
tangent space $T_pM$ is the real vector space of derivations at $p$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]), and the cotangent space is its
algebraic dual $T_p^*M:=(T_pM)^*$
([[def-cotangent-space-and-cotangent-bundle-as-a-disjoint-union]]).

A **covariant $2$-tensor at $p$** is a bilinear map
$A_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$. It is **symmetric** when
$A_p(v,w)=A_p(w,v)$ for all $v,w\in T_pM$, and **nondegenerate** when the only
$v\in T_pM$ with $A_p(v,w)=0$ for all $w\in T_pM$ is $v=0$.

A **smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$** is a family $A=(A_p)_{p\in M}$
assigning to each $p$ a covariant $2$-tensor $A_p$ at $p$, such that for every
chart $(U,x)$ of the maximal smooth atlas $[\mathcal A]$ the **component
functions**

$$A_{ab}(q):=A_q\!\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^a}\Big|_q,\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x^b}\Big|_q\right),\qquad q\in U,$$

are $C^\infty$ on $U$. Here $\partial/\partial x^a|_q$ is the coordinate
derivation at $q$ ([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]],
[[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the index
ranges over the label set $I_n=\{1,\dots,n\}$ (or the relabelled set
$I_4=\{0,1,2,3\}$ when $n=4$), and smoothness of the real-valued functions
$A_{ab}$ on the open set $U\subseteq M$ is the notion of
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]] applied to $M$ and
$\mathbb R$.

For a coordinate tuple $z\in x(U)$ define the **coordinate representative**
$A^x_{ab}(z):=A_{ab}(x^{-1}(z))$. When the argument is a coordinate tuple,
$A_{ab}(z)$ abbreviates this representative in the named chart; when it is a
point of $M$, it denotes the component function on the chart domain. Thus
$A_{ab}(x(y^{-1}(u)))$ in a change-of-coordinates formula means
$A^x_{ab}((x\circ y^{-1})(u))$, never evaluation of a function on $M$ at a
tuple. For $n=4$, $x^a$ and $\partial_a$ mean the original coordinate and
derivation labelled $a+1$, respectively; this relabels every slot and sum.
The label $0$ alone gives no coordinate vector a causal character.

Because the coordinate derivations at $q$ form a basis of $T_qM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), specifying
$A$ is the same as specifying the matrix of component functions in each chart;
[[lem-gr-covariant-two-tensor-transformation-law]] proves that the smoothness
requirement is independent of the chart used, so that the condition may be
checked on any smooth atlas of $M$, and derives the transformation law relating
components in two overlapping charts.

The field is **symmetric** when $A_p$ is symmetric for every $p\in M$, which in
a chart is the identity $A_{ab}=A_{ba}$ of component functions; it is
**nondegenerate** when $A_p$ is nondegenerate for every $p$, which in a chart is
the nonvanishing at every point of the polynomial function
$\det(A_{ab})$ of the components. The **matrix** of $A$ in a chart means the
matrix $\bigl(A_{ab}(q)\bigr)$ of its component functions at $q$.

**Convention.** In the four-dimensional case $n=4$ used in this library, indices
are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ with $0$ the time-coordinate label when such a coordinate is chosen, and we write
$A_{ab}$ for the components. A covariant $2$-tensor field is also called a
**$(0,2)$ tensor field**.

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold and let $A=(A_p)_{p\in M}$ be a family
assigning to each $p$ a covariant $2$-tensor at $p$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Suppose that the component
functions of $A$ are $C^\infty$ in the charts of one smooth atlas of $M$. Let
$(U,x)$ and $(V,y)$ be overlapping smooth charts of the maximal smooth atlas and
let $A_{cd}$ and $A'_{ab}$ denote their coordinate representatives in the
charts $x$ and $y$ as specified in [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]].
For $q\in U\cap V$ put $u=y(q)$ and write $x(u):=(x\circ y^{-1})(u)$. Then

$$A'_{ab}(u) = \sum_{c,d\in I_n}\frac{\partial x^c}{\partial y^a}(u)\,\frac{\partial x^d}{\partial y^b}(u)\,A_{cd}\bigl(x(u)\bigr),$$

where $\partial x^c/\partial y^a$ are the entries of the total derivative
$D(x\circ y^{-1})(u)$; $I_n$ is the label set of the supplier,
so in dimension four the sum runs from $0$ through $3$. In particular $A$ is a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field
on $M$: its components are $C^\infty$ in every chart of the maximal smooth
atlas.

Let $V$ be a $4$-dimensional real vector space ([[def-vector-space]],
[[def-dimension]]). A **Lorentz form** on $V$ is a symmetric bilinear form
$\eta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]])
such that

1. $\eta$ is nondegenerate: both radicals
   $\operatorname{rad}_L(\eta)=\{u:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }v\}$ and
   $\operatorname{rad}_R(\eta)=\{v:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }u\}$ are
   $\{0\}$ ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]);
   and
2. $\eta$ has **inertia** $(3,1,0)$: in some (equivalently, in every) basis of
   $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal, exactly three diagonal
   entries are positive, exactly one is negative, and none is zero
   ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]).

The inertia of a symmetric bilinear form is the triple $(p,q,r)$ of numbers of
positive, negative and zero diagonal entries of any diagonalizing basis, and it
is independent of the diagonalizing basis by Sylvester's law of inertia
([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]); hence clause 2
is a property of $\eta$ itself and not of a chosen basis. The **associated
quadratic form** of $\eta$ is

$$q(v):=\eta(v,v),\qquad v\in V .$$

A **Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$** is a pair $(V,\eta)$
consisting of a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$ and a Lorentz form $\eta$
on $V$; the name records that the diagonal normal form of $\eta$ has one
negative entry followed by three positive entries. No positive-definite
structure on $V$ is assumed or implied by this definition, and $q$ takes both
negative and positive values on nonzero vectors: a basis in which
$\eta$ is diagonal with diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$ exists by clause 2, and on
its first vector $q$ is $-1$, while on each of the other three it is $+1$.

Let $B$ be a symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional real vector space, and write $q(v):=B(v,v)$. The form is **positive definite** when $q(v)>0$ for every $v\ne0$, and **negative definite** when $q(v)<0$ for every $v\ne0$. The same terminology applies to the associated quadratic form.

Suppose a basis gives a diagonal matrix with $p$ positive diagonal entries, $q$ negative diagonal entries, and $r$ zero entries. Its **inertia** is the triple $(p,q,r)$, its **rank** is $p+q$, and its **signature** is $p-q$. Sylvester's law of inertia proves that this triple is independent of the diagonalizing basis, and therefore justifies the notation.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $c>0$ be a fixed real constant.
All curves below take values in $M$; the physical reading of $c$, of a
worldline as the history of a clock or body, and of the parameter values as
times is not part of this definition and is adopted separately in the
postulates of the framework.

**(a) Regularity classes.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with
nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A
**chart representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ for a smooth
chart $(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]).

- For $k\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ and an interior point $t_0\in I$, the map
  $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ at $t_0$** when there is a chart representative
  $x\circ\gamma$ defined near $t_0$ that is $C^k$ there in the componentwise
  Euclidean sense. This condition is independent of the chart: on the overlap
  of two chart representatives the transition map is smooth and the chain rule
  applies ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]],
  [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). If $t_0\in I$ is an
  included endpoint of $I$, the coordinate representative and its derivatives through order $k$
  are continuous up to $t_0$ on the relative interval
  $I\cap(t_0-\delta,t_0+\delta)$ for some $\delta>0$, with derivatives at
  $t_0$ taken one-sided. For $k=\infty$ this holds at every finite order.
  Merely possessing a one-sided secant tangent, as defined next, does not
  by itself make a curve $C^1$ at the endpoint. The map $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ on $I$** when it is $C^k$ at
  every point of $I$.

- Let $b\in\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon>0$. A curve
  $\gamma:(b-\varepsilon,b]\to M$ has **left tangent** $v\in T_{\gamma(b)}M$
  at $b$ when for one — equivalently every — chart $(U,x)$ around
  $\gamma(b)$, writing $v=\sum_{a=0}^{3}v^a\partial_a|_{\gamma(b)}$
  ([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the
  difference quotients satisfy
  $\bigl(x^a(\gamma(t))-x^a(\gamma(b))\bigr)/(t-b)\to v^a$ as $t\uparrow b$ for
  $a=0,1,2,3$. A **right tangent** at the left end of a curve is defined
  analogously with $t\downarrow b$. Chart independence is the one-sided
  chain-rule computation for the smooth transition maps
  ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

- A curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $a<b$ is **piecewise $C^1$** when there is a
  finite partition $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ such that for every $i$ the
  restriction of $\gamma$ to $[s_{i-1},s_i]$ is $C^1$ up to its included
  endpoints in the one-sided sense above: in every endpoint chart its
  component derivatives on the open piece have continuous one-sided limits,
  agreeing with its endpoint derivatives. Equivalently each piece has a
  $C^1$ extension to its closed parameter piece. In particular its right
  tangent at $s_{i-1}$ and left tangent at $s_i$ exist. Such a
  partition is called **admissible** for $\gamma$. The piece extensions give continuity at the
  corners; no agreement of the
  two one-sided tangents at a corner is required.

**(b) Velocity.** If $\gamma$ is $C^1$ at an interior point $t$, its
**velocity** $\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the velocity derivation of
[[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]] translated to the parameter
value $t$. In a chart around $\gamma(t)$ the velocity has the component
expression

$$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(x^a\circ\gamma\bigr)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)},$$

the coordinate expression of the derivation
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]). At an
included endpoint of the domain, $\gamma'$ means the corresponding one-sided
tangent of clause (a).

**(c) Timelike worldlines.** A **$C^k$ future timelike worldline** is a $C^k$
curve $\gamma:I\to M$ whose velocity $\gamma'(t)$ is future timelike at every
$t\in I$, in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]
and [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]: $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t))<0$
and $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),N_{\gamma(t)})<0$. A **piecewise-$C^1$ future
timelike worldline** is a piecewise-$C^1$ curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ whose
velocity at every point of each open piece and whose one-sided tangents at the
two ends of each piece are future timelike; the definition is applied to a map
on an arbitrary interval $I$ with nonempty interior by requiring it on every
compact subinterval of $I$. A future timelike velocity is in particular
nonzero, so every future timelike worldline is regular.

**(d) Proper time and length.** Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise-$C^1$
future timelike worldline and let $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ be an admissible
partition. On each open piece $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ the function

$$h_i(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}\bigl(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s)\bigr)}$$

is continuous and strictly positive: it is a finite sum of products of
continuous real functions in any chart around a point of the piece, as
$g_{ab}\circ\gamma$ and the components of $\gamma'$ are continuous
([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]],
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]]), and the
square root is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ ([[def-rational-power]],
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]). The continuous one-sided limits of the component derivatives, required
by the $C^1$ extension of each piece, and continuity of $g$ imply that
$h_i$ tends to the norm of the corresponding endpoint tangent. The future
timelike hypothesis on those tangents makes these limits strictly positive, and $h_i$ extends to a continuous function on
$[s_{i-1},s_i]$; hence it is Darboux integrable there
([[def-darboux-integral]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]). The
**proper-time increment** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is

$$\tau(b)-\tau(a):=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int_{s_{i-1}}^{s_i}h_i(s)\,ds,$$

and the **Lorentzian length** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is
$L_g(\gamma):=c\,(\tau(b)-\tau(a))$. For a base point $s_0\in I$ the
**proper-time function** $\tau:I\to\mathbb R$ of a future timelike worldline is
the function with $\tau(s_0)=0$ and $\tau(s)$ equal to the increment
from $s_0$ to $s$ when $s>s_0$, and minus the increment from $s$ to $s_0$
when $s<s_0$. That the increment is independent of the admissible
partition, so that $\tau$ is well defined, and that it is invariant under
increasing $C^1$ reparametrization are proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]]; the display is the
value for any admissible partition.

**(e) Four-velocity.** Let $\gamma$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ future timelike
worldline and let $t$ be a parameter value at which $\gamma$ is differentiable
(interior point of a piece, or an included endpoint with its one-sided
tangent). The **four-velocity** of $\gamma$ at $t$ is

$$U(t):=\frac{c\,\gamma'(t)}{\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t)\bigr)}}\in T_{\gamma(t)}M .$$

By construction $g_{\gamma(t)}(U(t),U(t))=-c^2$, and
$\gamma'(t)=\bigl(\sqrt{-g(\gamma',\gamma')}/c\bigr)U(t)$ with a strictly
positive scalar factor. If $U$ is written as the derivative of $\gamma$ with
respect to proper time, $U=d\gamma/d\tau$, this is a statement proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]], not part of the
present definition.

**(f) Scope.** Proper time, length and four-velocity are defined only for
future timelike worldlines. A null or spacelike curve receives no proper time
and no four-velocity from this definition, and no limiting or distributional
extension of the square-root integrand to such curves is asserted. The
parametrization of a worldline is part of the data and is arbitrary in this
definition: no affine parameter, no geodesic equation, no completeness or
extendability of the domain, and no measurement or clock reading is assumed.
Null and spacelike regularity classes are not defined here beyond the general
$C^k$ and piecewise-$C^1$ notions of clause (a), which make no causal
requirement.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$c>0$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

1. **Well-definedness and additivity of proper time.** Let
   $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ future timelike worldline
   ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]). Then the sum defining
   $\tau(b)-\tau(a)$ is the same for every admissible partition of $[a,b]$; it
   is written $\frac1c\int_a^b h$, where $h$ is the piecewise-defined
   proper-time density. For $a<c<b$,
   $\tau(b)-\tau(a)=\bigl(\tau(c)-\tau(a)\bigr)+\bigl(\tau(b)-\tau(c)\bigr)$.
   If $a<b$, the increment is strictly positive.

2. **Reparametrization and orientation, including subintervals.** Let
   $a'<b'$ and let $\varphi:[a',b']\to[a,b]$ be $C^1$ up to its included
   endpoints with nonzero derivative everywhere, including one-sided endpoint
   derivatives. Let $\tilde\gamma:=\gamma\circ\varphi$. Its derivative has
   constant sign and $\varphi$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto its actual image
   interval. If $\varphi'>0$, then $\tilde\gamma$ is a piecewise-$C^1$ future
   timelike worldline and
   $$\tilde\tau(b')-\tilde\tau(a')=\tau(\varphi(b'))-\tau(\varphi(a')).$$
   This equals $\tau(b)-\tau(a)$ when $\varphi(a')=a$ and $\varphi(b')=b$.
   If $\varphi'<0$, then $\tilde\gamma$ is a piecewise-$C^1$ **past** timelike
   traversal. Its unsigned density
   $\tilde h=\sqrt{-g(\tilde\gamma',\tilde\gamma')}$ obeys
   $$\frac1c\int_{a'}^{b'}\tilde h=\tau(\varphi(a'))-\tau(\varphi(b'))>0,$$
   whereas the oriented original difference
   $\tau(\varphi(b'))-\tau(\varphi(a'))$ is negative. For endpoint-reversing
   $\varphi(a')=b$, $\varphi(b')=a$, the latter equals
   $-\bigl(\tau(b)-\tau(a)\bigr)$. This negative oriented difference is not
   elapsed proper time for a future curve; parameter reversal reverses the
   causal direction. Non-surjective maps compare increments over their
   actual image interval, not over the whole original interval.

3. **Proper-time function and four-velocity.** Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a
   $C^1$ future timelike worldline on an interval with nonempty interior and
   let $\tau$ be its proper-time function based at $t_0\in I$
   ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]). Then $\tau$ is $C^1$ on
   $I$ with
   $$\tau'(t)=\frac{1}{c}\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t)\bigr)}>0,$$
   so $\tau$ is strictly increasing, and at every $t\in I$ the velocity,
   proper-time density and four-velocity satisfy
   $\gamma'(t)=\tau'(t)\,U(t)$ and $g_{\gamma(t)}(U(t),U(t))=-c^2$. If
   $\tau$ is strictly increasing on $I$ with image $J$, then the
   reparametrized curve $\gamma_\tau:=\gamma\circ(\tau|_I)^{-1}$ is a $C^1$
   future timelike worldline on $J$ with
   $$\gamma_\tau'(\sigma)=U\bigl(\tau^{-1}(\sigma)\bigr),\qquad g\bigl(\gamma_\tau'(\sigma),\gamma_\tau'(\sigma)\bigr)=-c^2 .$$
   The same formulas hold piece by piece for a piecewise-$C^1$ future
   timelike worldline, on each open piece and at its endpoints one-sided, with the two
   corner velocities kept distinct.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

For every point $p\in M$ and every smooth vector field $X$ on $M$, there is a
unique maximal integral curve $\gamma_p:I_p\to M$ of $X$ with $\gamma_p(0)=p$.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$. A smooth curve
$\gamma:I\to M$, defined on an interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, is an
**integral curve** of $X$ if

$$ \gamma'(t)=X_{\gamma(t)} $$

for every $t\in I$.

If $\gamma(0)=p$, then $\gamma$ is an integral curve of $X$ **through** $p$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, so that $TM$ carries its canonical smooth
structure. Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. A **smooth vector field** on $M$ is a
smooth section

$$ X:M\to TM $$

of the tangent-bundle projection $\pi:TM\to M$. Thus $\pi\circ X=\operatorname{id}_M$.

Equivalently, for each $p\in M$ the value $X(p)$ is a tangent vector in $T_pM$,
and the dependence on $p$ is smooth with respect to the canonical smooth
structure on $TM$.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Let $(M,\mathcal S)$ be a smooth $n$-manifold and let $U\subseteq M$ be open,
carrying the subspace topology. Then $U$ is a topological $n$-manifold. For
every smooth atlas $\mathcal A$ with $[\mathcal A]=\mathcal S$, the family of
restricted charts

$$\mathcal A|_U:=\bigl\{\,\bigl(V\cap U,\ \varphi|_{V\cap U}\bigr):(V,\varphi)\in\mathcal A\,\bigr\}.$$

is a smooth atlas on $U$, and the maximal atlas it generates is independent of
the presenting atlas $\mathcal A$: it depends only on the structure
$\mathcal S$. This maximal atlas is the **restricted smooth structure** of $U$.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

A **Riemannian metric** on a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $g$ such that $g_p(v,v)>0$ for every point $p$ and every nonzero $v\in T_pM$. A **Riemannian manifold** is the pair $(M,g)$.

This is a [[def-smooth-tensor-field]] giving a [[def-smooth-bundle-metric]] on $TM$. Dimension zero is allowed: its zero bilinear form is positive definite because there are no nonzero vectors. The empty manifold has its unique empty metric. Boundaries are allowed where stated, with smoothness understood up to the boundary.

Assume the inherited $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]);
the local calculations below use no further choice principle.

Let $\Sigma$ be a smooth manifold, let $\gamma$ be a Riemannian metric on
$\Sigma$ ([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]) and let
$\lambda>0$ be a constant. Write $\gamma_\lambda:=\lambda\gamma$ for the
rescaled metric. Then:

**(a) Connection.** The Levi-Civita connection of $\gamma_\lambda$ equals the
Levi-Civita connection of $\gamma$
([[prop-christoffel-formula-for-the-levi-civita-connection]]).

**(b) Curvature operator.** If $R_\lambda$ and $R$ are the curvature operators
of the two Levi-Civita connections in the convention
$R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$
([[prop-coordinate-formula-for-the-curvature-tensor]],
[[thm-curvature-is-a-type-one-three-tensor]]), then $R_\lambda=R$: the two
operators are equal as $(1,3)$-tensor fields.

**(c) Ricci and scalar curvature.** With the Ricci curvature of
[[def-ricci-curvature]] and the scalar curvature of [[def-scalar-curvature]],

$$\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma_\lambda)=\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma),\qquad S(\gamma_\lambda)=\lambda^{-1}S(\gamma).$$

**(d) Lowered curvature and sectional curvature.** With the Riemann four-tensor
of [[def-riemann-curvature-four-tensor]],

$$\operatorname{Rm}_{\gamma_\lambda}(X,Y,Z,W)=\lambda\,\operatorname{Rm}_\gamma(X,Y,Z,W),$$

and for every tangent two-plane $\sigma$ on which $\gamma$ is defined the
sectional curvature scales inversely,
$K_{\gamma_\lambda}(\sigma)=\lambda^{-1}K_\gamma(\sigma)$ ([[def-sectional-curvature]]).

This item assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as inherited through
[[def-constant-sectional-curvature-and-space-form]]; the pointwise tensor
arguments below use no further choice principle
([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $\Sigma$ be a smooth three-manifold and let $\gamma$ be a Riemannian
metric on $\Sigma$ ([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]), with
curvature operator $R$, Riemann four-tensor $\operatorname{Rm}$
([[def-riemann-curvature-four-tensor]]), Ricci curvature
$\operatorname{Ric}$ ([[def-ricci-curvature]]) and scalar curvature $S$
([[def-scalar-curvature]]). Let $k\in\mathbb R$. The following three
statements are equivalent:

**(a)** The metric $\gamma$ has constant sectional curvature $k$: every
tangent two-plane has sectional curvature $k$
([[def-constant-sectional-curvature-and-space-form]],
[[def-sectional-curvature]]).

**(b)** $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)=2k\gamma$ at every point of $\Sigma$; that
is the curvature condition for the real parameter $k$. When $\Sigma$ is
connected and boundaryless and $k\in\{-1,0,1\}$, it is precisely the
normalized spatial-model condition of [[def-gr-flrw-spatial-model]].

**(c)** $R(X,Y)Z=k\bigl(\gamma(Y,Z)X-\gamma(X,Z)Y\bigr)$ for all smooth vector
fields $X,Y,Z$ on $\Sigma$
([[prop-curvature-tensor-of-constant-sectional-curvature]]).

Whenever these hold, the scalar curvature is $S=6k$, and the trace-free Ricci
tensor vanishes, $\operatorname{Ric}_0=0$
([[def-kulkarni-nomizu-product-trace-free-ricci-and-weyl-curvature]]).

This item assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as inherited through the Riemannian
items cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]); no further choice principle is
used.

**(a) The datum.** Let $\Sigma$ be a connected smooth three-manifold without
boundary ([[def-smooth-manifold]]) and let $\gamma$ be a Riemannian metric on
$\Sigma$ ([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]). Let
$k\in\{-1,0,1\}$. The pair $(\Sigma,\gamma)$ is a **spatial model of constant
normalized curvature $k$**, with **normalized curvature parameter** $k$, when

$$\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)=2k\,\gamma\qquad\text{at every point of }\Sigma ,$$

where $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)$ is the Ricci curvature of $\gamma$
([[def-ricci-curvature]]). We then call $(\Sigma,\gamma,k)$ a **spatial model
datum**. The signs are named for orientation only: $k=+1$ is called the
**closed** or **positively curved** case, $k=0$ the **flat** case and $k=-1$
the **open** or **negatively curved** case; no topological content is attached
to these names by this definition.

**(b) Status of the condition.** The condition in (a) is pointwise and local.
It neither asserts nor implies that $\Sigma$ is complete, compact, simply
connected or geodesically complete, and it does not determine the global
model: this definition proves no classification theorem and this page assumes
none. In dimension three the condition is equivalent to the statement that
$\gamma$ has constant sectional curvature $k$; the companion lemma on
constant-curvature three-manifolds, recorded in the Remarks, proves that
equivalence. What is used by the cosmological deductions of this page is
exactly the Ricci form displayed in (a).

**(c) Normalization and scale.** The condition (a) fixes the numerical
curvature to $k\in\{-1,0,1\}$. For a constant $\lambda>0$, put
$\gamma'=\lambda^2\gamma$. Then

$$\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma')=\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)=2k\gamma=2(k/\lambda^2)\gamma',$$

and $K_{\gamma'}=k/\lambda^2$
([[lem-gr-constant-rescaling-preserves-levi-civita-and-curvature]]).
The sign is unchanged, but for $k\ne0$ the normalized condition (a) is
preserved only when $\lambda=1$; the flat condition is preserved for every
$\lambda>0$. Conversely, if $\operatorname{Ric}(h)=2\kappa h$ for a real
constant $\kappa\ne0$, the metric $\gamma=|\kappa|h$ satisfies
$\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)=2\operatorname{sgn}(\kappa)\gamma$ by the same
Ricci invariance, so it restores the normalization. A physical model assigns
its spatial length scale through the further factor in the model postulate.

**(d) Standard models.** For each $k\in\{-1,0,1\}$ at least one complete,
connected, boundaryless, simply connected model satisfying (a) is available:

- For $k=+1$, take the round unit sphere $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$ with its
  induced metric. Its constant curvature $+1$, completeness and connected
  boundaryless Riemannian structure are supplied by
  [[prop-round-sphere-model-geometry]] with $n=3$, $R=1$ (the curvature
  calculation is also [[ex-the-round-sphere-has-positive-constant-sectional-curvature]]);
  its simple connectedness is [[thm-higher-dimensional-spheres-are-simply-connected]].
- For $k=0$, take $\mathbb R^3$ with the standard metric. Its Riemannian
  structure and vanishing curvature are [[ex-euclidean-space-has-zero-curvature]].
  It is nonempty and convex, hence simply connected by
  [[thm-convex-subsets-have-trivial-fundamental-group]], and thus connected by
  [[thm-path-connected-implies-connected]]. For completeness, the constant
  metric coefficients give zero Christoffel symbols
  ([[prop-christoffel-formula-for-the-levi-civita-connection]]); for every
  initial position $p$ and velocity $v$, the all-time curve $t\mapsto p+tv$
  solves the coordinate geodesic equation
  ([[prop-coordinate-geodesic-equation]]). Uniqueness of the maximal geodesic
  ([[thm-existence-uniqueness-and-smooth-dependence-of-geodesics]]) identifies
  it with that curve, so every maximal geodesic has domain $\mathbb R$.
  Hopf–Rinow ([[thm-hopf-rinow]]) then gives metric completeness; its
  hypotheses hold because $\mathbb R^3$ is nonempty, connected and boundaryless.
- For $k=-1$, take the upper half-space $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x^3>0\}$ with
  $y=x^3$ and metric $y^{-2}\sum_{a=1}^3dx^a\otimes dx^a$.
  Its complete, connected, boundaryless, simply connected Riemannian
  structure and constant curvature $-1$ are exactly the $n=3$, $a=1$
  instance of [[prop-half-space-model-geometry]].

By the companion lemma recorded in the Remarks, constant sectional curvature
$k$ in dimension three gives $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)=2k\gamma$, so each
model satisfies (a) and each sign is realized. A model datum restricts to one
of these global standard models only when its postulate says so.

derivations.claim: (Smoothness and Lorentzian signature.) In a product chart $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ with $x^0=t$ the components of $g$ are the smooth functions displayed in [[def-gr-flrw-model-data]]: $g_{00}=-c^2$, $g_{0i}=0$, $g_{ij}=a(t)^2\gamma_{ij}(x)$. Product charts cover $M$ and their transition maps are products of the transition maps of $I$ and $\Sigma$, so by the transformation law [L1] the family $g$ is a smooth symmetric $(0,2)$-tensor field on $M$. At a point, the matrix of $g_p$ in the coordinate basis is block diagonal, $\operatorname{diag}(-c^2,\,a(t)^2(\gamma_{ij}(x))_{i,j=1}^{3})$. The $1\times1$ block has the single negative entry $-c^2$, and the $3\times3$ block is a positive multiple of the positive-definite matrix of $\gamma_x$; hence the diagonal entries of a diagonalization are one negative and three positive numbers, and $g_p$ is nondegenerate with inertia $(3,1,0)$. By [L2] this makes $g_p$ a Lorentz form at every point; by [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] the smooth field $g$ with these pointwise Lorentz forms is a Lorentzian metric of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on $M$. Since $g(N,N)=g_{00}=-c^2<0$ at every point, [L3] makes $N=\partial_t$ a time orientation and $(M,g,N)$ a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold.

(The comoving congruence and the comoving curves.) By step 1.1 the manifold $(M,g,N)$ is time-oriented smooth Lorentzian, so the causal vocabulary of [L3] applies. The field $n=c^{-1}\partial_t$ is a smooth vector field; its metric pairing is $g(n,n)=c^{-2}g(\partial_t,\partial_t)=c^{-2}(-c^2)=-1$, and $g(n,N)=-c<0$. Hence $n$ is a future-directed unit timelike vector field, i.e. a smooth future-directed unit timelike congruence. For fixed $x\in\Sigma$ the smooth curve $\gamma_x:I\to M$, $\gamma_x(t)=(t,x)$ has tangent $\partial_t=cn$; its image is $I\times\{x\}$ and its velocity satisfies $g(\gamma_x',\gamma_x')=-c^2<0$ and $g(\gamma_x',N)=-c^2<0$, so it is a future timelike worldline. For $(t_0,x)\in M$, the curve $\eta_{t_0,x}(s)=(t_0+s/c,x)$ on $c(I-t_0)$ has derivative $c^{-1}\partial_t=n$, so it is the integral curve of $n$ through that point by [L5]. Any extension would still satisfy $dt/ds=c^{-1}$ and constant spatial coordinates, hence would leave $I\times\Sigma$ beyond this interval; its domain is therefore maximal. The curve $\gamma_x$ is the cosmic-time reparametrization $s=c(t-t_0)$ of this same observer trajectory, with velocity $cn$.

(Cosmic time is proper time.) For the comoving curve $\gamma_x$ of step 2.1, the proper-time density of [L4] is $h(t)=\sqrt{-g(\gamma_x'(t),\gamma_x'(t))}=\sqrt{c^2}=c$, a constant. Hence for $t_0<t_1$ in $I$, the proper-time increment is $c^{-1}\int_{t_0}^{t_1}c\,dt=t_1-t_0$ by [L4]; in particular the parameter $t$ is proper time along $\gamma_x$ up to the choice of zero. The physical four-velocity, defined as the derivative of the worldline with respect to this proper time ([[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]]), is therefore $U=d\gamma_x/dt=\partial_t=cn$, with $g(U,U)=-c^2$.

(Slices, orthogonality and the scaled spatial curvature.) Fix $t_0\in I$. The map $\iota_{t_0}:\Sigma\to M$, $\iota_{t_0}(x)=(t_0,x)$, is a smooth embedding onto the embedded submanifold $\{t_0\}\times\Sigma$. In a product chart the differential of $\iota_{t_0}$ sends $\partial_i|_x$ to $\partial_i|_{(t_0,x)}$, so the pullback components are $(\iota_{t_0}^*g)_{ij}=g_{ij}(t_0,x)=a(t_0)^2\gamma_{ij}(x)$: a smooth, symmetric, positive definite field, hence a Riemannian metric $\gamma_{t_0}=a(t_0)^2\gamma$ by [L6]. Moreover $g(n,\partial_i)=0$ for $i=1,2,3$ because $g_{0i}=0$ and $n$ has no spatial component: the congruence is orthogonal to every slice. Finally, by [L7] the constant rescaling gives $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma_{t_0})=\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)=2k\gamma=\frac{2k}{a(t_0)^2}\,\gamma_{t_0}$, so $\gamma_{t_0}$ satisfies the Ricci form with parameter $k/a(t_0)^2$; the equivalence [L7] turns this into constant sectional curvature $k/a(t_0)^2$.

(Conclusion.) Steps 1.1 and 2.1 establish clauses (a) and (b), step 3.1 establishes the proper-time and four-velocity statements of (b), and step 3.2 establishes clause (c). The proofs used only the displayed component functions, the pointwise algebra of symmetric bilinear forms and the cited general facts; no field equation and no choice beyond the inherited $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of the suppliers was used.

boundaries.reason: The time interval I is nonempty by the definition of the datum and all claims are pointwise or along the explicitly given curves γ_x on I; no empty family of observers, charts or indices is quantified.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1: the time block entry is −c^2 with c > 0 and the spatial block is a(t_0)^2 times a positive-definite matrix with a(t_0) > 0, so every inverted quantity is nonzero; the curvature parameter k = 0 is included through the Ricci equivalence of [L7] in step 3.2.

boundaries.reason: The lemma makes no one-particle, one-dimensional or singleton-slice assertion beyond the single fixed slice t_0 in step 3.2, which is a free parameter of that step rather than a degenerate case.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1: g_p is proved nondegenerate at every point by exhibiting the inertia (3,1,0) in the product basis; the degenerate case is excluded by proof rather than assumed.
step 3.1: proper-time increments are computed for t_0 < t_1 in the open interval I with the conventions of [L4]; no value at an endpoint of I is used, because I is open.

step 3.2: for each fixed t_0 the single slice inclusion ι_{t_0} is fixed; no simultaneous selection over t_0 or over the points of Σ is made, and the only inherited assumption is AC_ω of the tangent-bundle suppliers.

boundaries.reason: The lemma asserts several independent clauses, not an equivalence, so there is no forward implication to check separately.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed five steps against product data, Lorentz inertia, tensor transformation, causal orientation, proper-time and maximal-integral-curve suppliers. Positive a and c yield one negative and three positive directions, g(n,n)=-1, and proper-time increment t1-t0. The curve parameter s has exact maximal domain c(I-t0); the slice pullback is explicitly a(t0)^2 gamma and positive definite. Reader L6 repair is sound: an arbitrary Lorentzian pullback need not be a metric. Amended step 2.1: the image of gamma_x is I times {x}, not the singleton {t} times {x}.
