vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

derivations.claim: (Part (a): equivalence of the two systems in the presence of (F).) Assume (F) holds on $I$, and multiply it by $3$: $\frac{3(\dot a^2+kc^2)}{a^2}=\frac{8\pi G_N\varepsilon}{c^2}+\Lambda c^2$; equivalently $\frac{\dot a^2+kc^2}{c^2}=\frac{8\pi G_N a^2\varepsilon}{3c^4}+\frac{\Lambda a^2}{3}$. Substituting this into the left-hand side of (S) gives $-\frac{2a\ddot a}{c^2}-\frac{\dot a^2+kc^2}{c^2}+\Lambda a^2=-\frac{2a\ddot a}{c^2}-\frac{8\pi G_Na^2\varepsilon}{3c^4}-\frac{\Lambda a^2}{3}+\Lambda a^2=-\frac{2a\ddot a}{c^2}-\frac{8\pi G_Na^2\varepsilon}{3c^4}+\frac{2\Lambda a^2}{3}$. Hence, under (F), equation (S) is equivalent to $-\frac{2a\ddot a}{c^2}-\frac{8\pi G_Na^2\varepsilon}{3c^4}+\frac{2\Lambda a^2}{3}=\frac{8\pi G_Na^2p}{c^4}$; multiplying by $\frac{c^2}{a^2}$ and dividing by $2$ gives $-\frac{\ddot a}{a}=\frac{4\pi G_N}{c^2}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{3}+p\right)-\frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}$, that is, $\frac{\ddot a}{a}=-\frac{4\pi G_N}{3c^2}(\varepsilon+3p)+\frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}$, which is (A). Each step is an equivalence (multiplication by the nonzero numbers $\frac{c^2}{a^2}$ and $2$, and rearrangement), so (F) and (S) hold exactly when (F) and (A) hold.

(Part (b): differentiation where $H\neq0$.) Assume (F) and (C) on $I$, fix $t_0\in I$ with $H(t_0)\neq0$. The functions on both sides of (F) are smooth on $I$, so differentiating the identity and using [L2] on the terms $\frac{kc^2}{a^2}$ and $H^2=\frac{\dot a^2}{a^2}$ gives $2H\dot H-\frac{2kc^2\dot a}{a^3}=\frac{8\pi G_N}{3c^2}\dot\varepsilon$ at every point of $I$; since $\frac{\dot a}{a}=H$ this is $2H\left(\dot H-\frac{kc^2}{a^2}\right)=\frac{8\pi G_N}{3c^2}\dot\varepsilon$. Substituting the continuity equation (C), $\dot\varepsilon=-3H(\varepsilon+p)$, and dividing by the nonzero number $2H(t_0)$ yields $\dot H-\frac{kc^2}{a^2}=-\frac{4\pi G_N}{c^2}(\varepsilon+p)$ at $t_0$. By [L3], $\frac{\ddot a}{a}=\dot H+H^2$ at $t_0$, so $\frac{\ddot a}{a}=\frac{kc^2}{a^2}+H^2-\frac{4\pi G_N}{c^2}(\varepsilon+p)$; substituting (F) for the sum $\frac{kc^2}{a^2}+H^2=\frac{8\pi G_N\varepsilon}{3c^2}+\frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}$ gives $\frac{\ddot a}{a}=\frac{8\pi G_N\varepsilon}{3c^2}-\frac{4\pi G_N}{c^2}(\varepsilon+p)+\frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}=-\frac{4\pi G_N}{3c^2}(\varepsilon+3p)+\frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}$, which is (A) at $t_0$. This proves part (b) at every point where $H$ does not vanish; the division by $H(t_0)$ is the only use of the hypothesis, and no conclusion is drawn at its zeros.

boundaries.reason: The datum has a nonempty time interval and the equations are pointwise at each t ∈ I; no empty family, empty sum or empty chart set is quantified.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1: the equivalence multiplies only by the nonzero numbers c^2/a^2 and 2, with a > 0; step 2.1 divides by H(t_0) under the explicit hypothesis H(t_0) ≠ 0 and makes no claim at zeros of H, as the statement records.

boundaries.reason: No one-dimensional or single-equation reduction is claimed beyond the four listed equations; the proposition compares two presentations of the same system.

boundaries.evidence: step 2.1: the derivation from (F) and (C) degenerates exactly at H(t_0) = 0, and the proposition excludes that case by hypothesis instead of dividing by a possibly vanishing quantity; step 1.1 covers all values of ε, p and ä.

boundaries.reason: All equations are identities at interior points t_0 ∈ I of the open interval; no endpoint of I is evaluated and no one-sided limit occurs.

boundaries.evidence: step 2.1: H(t_0) is a single real number and the division is a scalar operation; no selection from a family occurs anywhere in the proof.
step 1.1: starting from (F), the substitutions transform (S) into (A) and every step is reversible, so the forward direction of clause (a) is covered; clause (b) is verified in step 2.1.
step 1.1: the same reversible chain read backwards transforms (A) into (S) under (F), so the reverse direction of clause (a) is covered.

risk_review.notes: Both proof steps independently checked using the exact F,A,C,S equations and the product, quotient and chain rule statements. Substitution under F is reversible since c and a are positive. Differentiated F and C imply A precisely at nonzero H; no division or assertion at a zero of H. Smoothness on a nonempty open interval supplies the derivative and limit-point hypotheses. No defect, no edit.

citations.quote:
Adopt as the geometry and matter content of a **homogeneous cosmological
model** of the classical gravitational framework, to be used together with
[[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]],
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]] and the field law of
[[post-gr-einstein-field-law]], the following assumptions.

**(i) Spacetime geometry.** The model's spacetime is an FLRW model datum
$(I,\Sigma,\gamma,k,a)$ with the framework's conversion constant $c>0$, its
metric $g=-c^2dt^2+a(t)^2\gamma$ and its comoving congruence
$n=c^{-1}\partial_t$ ([[def-gr-flrw-model-data]],
[[lem-gr-flrw-metric-and-comoving-data]]). The spatial model
$(\Sigma,\gamma,k)$ is one of the standard complete simply connected models of
[[def-gr-flrw-spatial-model]] clause (d), with normalized curvature parameter
$k\in\{-1,0,1\}$: the round unit three-sphere for $k=+1$, Euclidean space for
$k=0$, or hyperbolic three-space for $k=-1$; by
[[lem-gr-constant-curvature-three-manifold-ricci]] each of these carries
constant sectional curvature $k$ and $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)=2k\gamma$.
The name **homogeneous and isotropic cosmological model** denotes here the
explicit standard-spatial-model FLRW ansatz just specified. Its operative
geometric assumptions are the chosen global standard model, the displayed
metric and the curvature condition; the deductions do not use an additional
undefined symmetry premise. The identification of the coordinate
$t$ with the readings of ideal comoving clocks is not part of this clause: it
is the separate clock rule of [[post-gr-ideal-clocks-and-free-fall]], applied
only where a physical clock reading is asserted. The
mathematical content used by the deductions of this page is the FLRW form
displayed above together with the curvature condition; no classification
theorem, and no transitivity statement about isometry groups, is proved or
used here.

**(ii) Matter content.** Exactly one of the following two sectors is adopted.

- **Vacuum sector.** No matter is present: the model's stress-energy tensor is
  the zero tensor, $\varepsilon=p=0$.
- **Comoving perfect-fluid sector.** The model's matter is a perfect-fluid
  model $(\varepsilon,p,n_F)$ on the matter domain $U:=M$, the model's whole
  spacetime, in the sense of [[def-gr-perfect-fluid-matter-model]]: that is,
  $U=M$ is the nonempty open domain, $\varepsilon$ and $p$ are the smooth
  rest energy density and pressure on it, and the fluid's unit timelike
  four-velocity field $n_F$ is assumed to be the comoving congruence
  $n=c^{-1}\partial_t$ of clause (i). The density and pressure are assumed
  **homogeneous**, that is, functions of cosmic time alone:
  $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(t)$ and $p=p(t)$ in the product charts, with
  values in the units of [[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]. The
  model additionally adopts an **explicit equation of state**, one of:
  a barotropic relation $p=P(\varepsilon)$ with $P$ a smooth real function
  defined on an open interval containing the range of $\varepsilon$; or the
  constant-parameter relation $p=w\varepsilon$ with a real constant $w$ and
  the stated domain of positive $\varepsilon$. The equation of state is an
  adopted constitutive restriction, not a consequence of the field law.
  The fluid stress-energy $T_{ab}=(\varepsilon+p)n_an_b+pg_{ab}$ is the
  gravitating source in $G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=(8\pi G_N/c^4)T_{ab}$
  ([[post-gr-einstein-field-law]]). The scale factor and fluid data must
  jointly satisfy that law when a solution is claimed; the fluid is not
  treated as test matter on a separately prescribed background.

**(iii) Status, scope and exclusions.** Clauses (i) and (ii) are adopted
assumptions of the model. They are not derived from the field law, from
mathematical symmetry, or from observation; the symmetry of the ansatz
motivates but does not prove them, and no claim is made that any actual
cosmological system is exactly homogeneous, isotropic, comoving or
barotropic. The model contains no observed value: the scale factor, the
densities, the parameters $k,\Lambda,w$ and the spacetime interval are model
data, and every conclusion conditional on the model inherits the idealizations
listed in the physical scope of this item. Anisotropic stresses, heat flow and
dissipation, spatial inhomogeneities and perturbations, distributional or
lower-dimensional sources, non-smooth fields and quantum effects lie outside
the model and require additional content. Comparisons of the model's
predictions with reported observations test the combined model — geometry,
matter content, field law and the observation and analysis assumptions — and
agreement is evidence about that combination, not a proof of this postulate.

Let $(I,\Sigma,\gamma,k,a)$ be an FLRW model datum with conversion constant
$c>0$, with spacetime $M=I\times\Sigma$, metric $g=-c^2dt^2+a(t)^2\gamma$ and
comoving congruence $n=c^{-1}\partial_t$
([[def-gr-flrw-model-data]], [[def-gr-flrw-spatial-model]]). Then:

**(a)** The field $g$ is a smooth Lorentzian metric of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
on $M$, and $N:=\partial_t$ satisfies $g(N,N)=-c^2<0$ at every point; hence
$(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]).

**(b)** The comoving congruence $n=c^{-1}\partial_t$ is a smooth
future-directed unit timelike vector field on $M$: $g(n,n)=-1$ and
$g(n,N)=-c<0$ at every point
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Its maximal integral
curve through $(t_0,x)$ is $\eta_{t_0,x}(s)=(t_0+s/c,x)$ on
$c(I-t_0)=\{c(t-t_0):t\in I\}$. Reparametrizing by cosmic time gives the
**comoving curve** $\gamma_x(t):=(t,x)$ on $I$; each is a future timelike
worldline whose parameter $t$ is its proper time up to an additive constant:
for $t_0,t_1\in I$ with $t_0<t_1$, the proper-time increment between
$\gamma_x(t_0)$ and $\gamma_x(t_1)$ is $t_1-t_0$
([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]],
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]]). The physical
four-velocity of a comoving observer is $U=\partial_t=cn$, with $g(U,U)=-c^2$.

**(c)** The congruence $n$ is $g$-orthogonal to the spatial slices: for every
$t_0\in I$, the slice inclusion $\iota_{t_0}:\Sigma\to M$, $x\mapsto(t_0,x)$,
is a smooth embedding, the pullback $\iota_{t_0}^*g=a(t_0)^2\gamma$ is a
Riemannian metric on $\Sigma$, and $g(n,\iota_{t_0*}v)=0$ for every
$v\in T_x\Sigma$. Moreover the slice metric $\gamma_{t_0}:=a(t_0)^2\gamma$
has Ricci curvature $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma_{t_0})=2k\gamma$ and constant
sectional curvature $k/a(t_0)^2$
([[lem-gr-constant-rescaling-preserves-levi-civita-and-curvature]],
[[lem-gr-constant-curvature-three-manifold-ricci]]).

This item assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the tangent-bundle and
manifold-product suppliers cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]); no further
choice principle is used.

**(a) Data.** Let $c>0$ be a real constant. An **FLRW model datum with
conversion constant $c$** is a tuple

$$(I,\Sigma,\gamma,k,a)$$

consisting of:

1. a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, the **time interval**
   ([[def-interval]]);
2. a spatial model datum $(\Sigma,\gamma,k)$: a connected smooth
   three-manifold $\Sigma$ without boundary, a Riemannian metric $\gamma$ on
   $\Sigma$, and a normalized curvature parameter $k\in\{-1,0,1\}$ with
   $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)=2k\gamma$
   ([[def-gr-flrw-spatial-model]], [[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]],
   [[def-smooth-manifold]]);
3. a **scale factor**: a smooth map $a:I\to(0,\infty)$, with values in the open
   interval of strictly positive reals
   ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]).

Its **spacetime** is the product manifold $M:=I\times\Sigma$ with the product
smooth structure
([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]]),
a smooth four-manifold without boundary. We write $t:M\to I$ for the first
coordinate function, the **cosmic time**, and $\dot a:=\frac{d}{dt}a$ for the
derivative of the scale factor ([[def-derivative]]).

**(b) The FLRW metric.** In product charts $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ with $x^0=t$,
where $(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ is a smooth chart of $\Sigma$, define the component functions

$$g_{00}:=-c^2,\qquad g_{0i}:=g_{i0}:=0,\qquad g_{ij}:=a(t)^2\gamma_{ij},\qquad i,j\in\{1,2,3\}.$$

These functions are smooth on the chart domain, and they define a smooth
symmetric covariant two-tensor field $g$ on $M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]): the component transformation
law is that of a symmetric $(0,2)$-tensor because the definitions agree on
chart overlaps, the time component is constant and the spatial components are
multiplied by the common smooth factor $a(t)^2$. The field $g$ is the
**FLRW metric** of the datum; we write the standard informal display
$g=-c^2\,dt^2+a(t)^2\,\gamma$, meaning the symmetric tensor $-c^2\,dt\otimes dt+a(t)^2\gamma$.
That $g$ is a Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ on $M$ and that the coordinate field $\partial_t$ is a time
orientation for it are not asserted by this definition but proved in
[[lem-gr-flrw-metric-and-comoving-data]] on this page; the same holds for the
clauses below that use the metric's causal classification.

**(c) Comoving congruence and cosmic time direction.** The **comoving
congruence** of the datum is the smooth vector field
$n:=c^{-1}\partial_t$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). By
[[lem-gr-flrw-metric-and-comoving-data]] the field $n$ is a smooth
future-directed unit timelike field, $g(n,n)=-1$, and the **comoving
observers** of the datum are its maximal integral curves; in product
coordinates the integral curve through $(t_0,x)$ is
$s\mapsto(t_0+s/c,x)$ on $c(I-t_0)$. Its proper-time parametrization is the
**comoving curve** $t\mapsto(t,x)$ on $I$, with constant spatial coordinate
$x\in\Sigma$ and velocity $U=cn=\partial_t$.

**(d) Hubble parameter and expansion.** The **Hubble parameter** of the datum
is the smooth function

$$H:=\frac{\dot a}{a}:I\to\mathbb R .$$

No field equation, no matter content, no equation of state, no measured value
and no claim about nature is part of this definition: an FLRW model datum is a
geometric object, and the physical reading of $c$, of $t$ as a clock reading,
of $n$ as the matter rest congruence and of $H$ as an expansion rate is
recorded in the physical postulates of the framework, not here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and let
$U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open matter domain
([[prop-an-open-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold-has-a-canonical-restricted-smooth-structure]]).

**(a) Data.** A **perfect-fluid model** on $U$ is a triple $(\varepsilon,p,n)$
consisting of two smooth functions $\varepsilon,p:U\to\mathbb R$, the **rest
energy density** and the **pressure**, and a smooth future-directed unit
timelike vector field $n$ on $U$ with $g_p(n_p,n_p)=-1$ and
$g_p(n_p,N_p)<0$ at every $p$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). No positivity of
$\varepsilon$ or of $p$ is required or implied. A model may carry the
additional data of an **equation of state**: a function
$P:D_P\to\mathbb R$ on a subset $D_P\subseteq\mathbb R$ with
$\varepsilon(U)\subseteq D_P$, together with the relation $p=P(\varepsilon)$;
the relation is a further assumption and is not part of the basic triple.

**(b) Stress-energy tensor and derived fields.** The model's
**stress-energy tensor** is

$$T^{ab}:=(\varepsilon+p)n^an^b+p\,g^{ab},$$

a smooth symmetric contravariant $2$-tensor field ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]). The **comoving
derivative**, **expansion** and **acceleration** of $n$ are

$$D f:=n^a\partial_af\quad(f\in C^\infty(U)),\qquad \vartheta:=\nabla_an^a,\qquad a^b:=n^a\nabla_an^b ,$$

and the **rest-space projection** is the smooth tensor field

$$h^{ab}:=g^{ab}+n^an^b .$$

The physical reading of $\varepsilon$ and $p$ as a rest-frame energy density
and pressure, and their units, are fixed by the framework's matter postulate,
not by this definition.

**(c) Fluid equations.** The **perfect-fluid equations** on $U$ are

$$D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+p)\vartheta=0,\qquad (\varepsilon+p)a^b+h^{ba}\partial_ap=0 .$$

That the stress-energy tensor is divergence-free if and only if these two
equations hold is proved in
[[prop-gr-dust-and-perfect-fluid-conservation-equations]]; the definition
asserts neither divergence-freedom nor the equations.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open subset, the **matter domain** of the model,
carrying the restricted smooth structure of
[[prop-an-open-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold-has-a-canonical-restricted-smooth-structure]].

A **stress-energy tensor field** on $U$ for the model is a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field $T$ on $U$ in the sense of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]: at every $p\in U$, $T_p$ is a
symmetric bilinear form $T_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$ varying smoothly with
$p$, with component functions $T_{ab}=T(\partial_a,\partial_b)$ in every smooth
chart of $U$. No nondegeneracy of $T_p$ is required or implied; in particular
$T_p$ may have radical, as it does for a dust model whose stress-energy form
vanishes on a hyperplane.

**Unit and observer reading.** At a point choose a $g_p$-orthonormal ordered
basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with $e_0$ future-directed, meaning
$g(e_0,N)<0$, and $g(e_A,e_B)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{AB}$.
Such a basis is obtained from an orthonormal basis by reversing its timelike
member if necessary. Write $T_{AB}=T(e_A,e_B)$ and $n=e_0$.
Every $T_{AB}$ has the energy-density reading
$\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}$ of [[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]].
The energy density for this observer is $\rho_n=T_{00}$; the spatial component
$\phi^i=-T_{0i}=T^{0i}$ gives the SI energy-flux component
$q_n^i=c\phi^i$ in $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}$ and the SI momentum-density
component $(p_n)_i=\phi^i/c$ in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-2}\mathrm s^{-1}$. The stress is $T_{ij}$ in
$\mathrm{Pa}=\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}$, $i,j=1,2,3$.
Thus the off-diagonal tensor entries themselves have energy-density units;
their flux and momentum readings require the stated sign and $c$ factors.
These names and readings interpret a prescribed tensor and a prescribed
future observer, and assert no actual measurement. Different future
orthonormal frames generally give different components, related by the
corresponding Lorentz change of basis.

**Relation to the matter model.** This item defines the slot that a matter
model fills. The identity of $T$ for a given model — its expression in terms of
the model's fields and its equation of motion — comes from that model and is
not part of this definition; for a model derived from an action, $T$ is the
Hilbert stress-energy tensor of that action, while a model that prescribes $T$
by hand is a separate source model subject to the consistency conditions of the
adopted gravitational field law. Nothing here asserts that a prescribed smooth
symmetric $T$ is realized by any matter model, that $T$ is conserved, or that
$T$ satisfies any positivity condition; conservation and the energy conditions
are separate statements, the latter defined separately in this framework.

**Scope limitations.** The definition is confined to the smooth branch: a
matter distribution whose density fails to be smooth across a surface, a
distributional point source, or a source supported on a hypersurface is not a
stress-energy tensor field of this definition, and such configurations require
additional distributional or junction mathematics not supplied here. The
matter domain $U$ is an idealization of the region occupied by matter; the
model may also include matter sources described on all of $M$ or on a union of
several such domains.

Let $(I,\Sigma,\gamma,k,a)$ be an FLRW model datum with conversion constant
$c>0$, with spacetime $M=I\times\Sigma$ and metric $g$
([[def-gr-flrw-model-data]], [[def-gr-flrw-spatial-model]]), let $\nabla$ be
its metric-selected connection, and let $R^a{}_{bcd}$,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ be the curvature components, Ricci
tensor, scalar curvature and Einstein tensor of $\nabla$
([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]). In a product chart
$(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ with $x^0=t$, with $\dot a$ the derivative of the scale
factor and $H=\dot a/a$:

**(a)** $\operatorname{Ric}_{00}=-\dfrac{3\ddot a}{a}$,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{0i}=0$, and
$\operatorname{Ric}_{ij}=\Bigl(\dfrac{a\ddot a+2\dot a^2}{c^2}+2k\Bigr)\gamma_{ij}$
for $i,j\in\{1,2,3\}$;

**(b)** $S=6\Bigl(\dfrac{\ddot a}{ac^2}+\dfrac{H^2}{c^2}+\dfrac{k}{a^2}\Bigr)$;

**(c)** $G_{00}=\dfrac{3(\dot a^2+kc^2)}{a^2}$, $G_{0i}=0$, and
$G_{ij}=-\Bigl(\dfrac{2a\ddot a+\dot a^2}{c^2}+k\Bigr)\gamma_{ij}$ for
$i,j\in\{1,2,3\}$.

All displayed component functions are smooth on the chart domain; the
identities are equalities of the components of the respective tensor fields
in the product chart and hold at every point.

Let $(I,\Sigma,\gamma,k,a)$ be an FLRW model datum with conversion constant
$c>0$, with spacetime $M=I\times\Sigma$, metric $g$, comoving congruence
$n=c^{-1}\partial_t$ and Hubble parameter $H=\dot a/a$
([[def-gr-flrw-model-data]], [[lem-gr-flrw-metric-and-comoving-data]]), and
let $\nabla$ be the metric-selected connection of $g$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]). Then:

**(a)** $\nabla_{\partial_t}\partial_t=0$ and $\nabla_nn=0$; consequently the
comoving curves are geodesics of $\nabla$ with affine parameter $t$, the
parameter $t$ is their proper time, and, when $\Sigma\ne\varnothing$, $n$ is a geodesic unit timelike
observer congruence in the sense of
[[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]).

**(b)** The **expansion** of the comoving congruence
$\vartheta:=\nabla_an^a$
([[def-gr-perfect-fluid-matter-model]] clause (b),
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]) is the constant-in-space
function

$$\vartheta=\frac{3H}{c}.$$

**(c)** For the physical four-velocity field $U=\partial_t=cn$ of the comoving
observers, $\nabla_aU^a=3H$, so that
$H=\tfrac13\nabla_aU^a$; the acceleration of the comoving congruence,
$a^b:=n^a\nabla_an^b$, vanishes identically
([[def-gr-perfect-fluid-matter-model]] clause (b)).

Adopt as the geometry and matter content of a **homogeneous cosmological
model** of the classical gravitational framework, to be used together with
[[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]],
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]] and the field law of
[[post-gr-einstein-field-law]], the following assumptions.

**(i) Spacetime geometry.** The model's spacetime is an FLRW model datum
$(I,\Sigma,\gamma,k,a)$ with the framework's conversion constant $c>0$, its
metric $g=-c^2dt^2+a(t)^2\gamma$ and its comoving congruence
$n=c^{-1}\partial_t$ ([[def-gr-flrw-model-data]],
[[lem-gr-flrw-metric-and-comoving-data]]). The spatial model
$(\Sigma,\gamma,k)$ is one of the standard complete simply connected models of
[[def-gr-flrw-spatial-model]] clause (d), with normalized curvature parameter
$k\in\{-1,0,1\}$: the round unit three-sphere for $k=+1$, Euclidean space for
$k=0$, or hyperbolic three-space for $k=-1$; by
[[lem-gr-constant-curvature-three-manifold-ricci]] each of these carries
constant sectional curvature $k$ and $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)=2k\gamma$.
The name **homogeneous and isotropic cosmological model** denotes here the
explicit standard-spatial-model FLRW ansatz just specified. Its operative
geometric assumptions are the chosen global standard model, the displayed
metric and the curvature condition; the deductions do not use an additional
undefined symmetry premise. The identification of the coordinate
$t$ with the readings of ideal comoving clocks is not part of this clause: it
is the separate clock rule of [[post-gr-ideal-clocks-and-free-fall]], applied
only where a physical clock reading is asserted. The
mathematical content used by the deductions of this page is the FLRW form
displayed above together with the curvature condition; no classification
theorem, and no transitivity statement about isometry groups, is proved or
used here.

**(ii) Matter content.** Exactly one of the following two sectors is adopted.

- **Vacuum sector.** No matter is present: the model's stress-energy tensor is
  the zero tensor, $\varepsilon=p=0$.
- **Comoving perfect-fluid sector.** The model's matter is a perfect-fluid
  model $(\varepsilon,p,n_F)$ on the matter domain $U:=M$, the model's whole
  spacetime, in the sense of [[def-gr-perfect-fluid-matter-model]]: that is,
  $U=M$ is the nonempty open domain, $\varepsilon$ and $p$ are the smooth
  rest energy density and pressure on it, and the fluid's unit timelike
  four-velocity field $n_F$ is assumed to be the comoving congruence
  $n=c^{-1}\partial_t$ of clause (i). The density and pressure are assumed
  **homogeneous**, that is, functions of cosmic time alone:
  $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(t)$ and $p=p(t)$ in the product charts, with
  values in the units of [[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]. The
  model additionally adopts an **explicit equation of state**, one of:
  a barotropic relation $p=P(\varepsilon)$ with $P$ a smooth real function
  defined on an open interval containing the range of $\varepsilon$; or the
  constant-parameter relation $p=w\varepsilon$ with a real constant $w$ and
  the stated domain of positive $\varepsilon$. The equation of state is an
  adopted constitutive restriction, not a consequence of the field law.
  The fluid stress-energy $T_{ab}=(\varepsilon+p)n_an_b+pg_{ab}$ is the
  gravitating source in $G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=(8\pi G_N/c^4)T_{ab}$
  ([[post-gr-einstein-field-law]]). The scale factor and fluid data must
  jointly satisfy that law when a solution is claimed; the fluid is not
  treated as test matter on a separately prescribed background.

**(iii) Status, scope and exclusions.** Clauses (i) and (ii) are adopted
assumptions of the model. They are not derived from the field law, from
mathematical symmetry, or from observation; the symmetry of the ansatz
motivates but does not prove them, and no claim is made that any actual
cosmological system is exactly homogeneous, isotropic, comoving or
barotropic. The model contains no observed value: the scale factor, the
densities, the parameters $k,\Lambda,w$ and the spacetime interval are model
data, and every conclusion conditional on the model inherits the idealizations
listed in the physical scope of this item. Anisotropic stresses, heat flow and
dissipation, spatial inhomogeneities and perturbations, distributional or
lower-dimensional sources, non-smooth fields and quantum effects lie outside
the model and require additional content. Comparisons of the model's
predictions with reported observations test the combined model — geometry,
matter content, field law and the observation and analysis assumptions — and
agreement is evidence about that combination, not a proof of this postulate.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$ and let $U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open
matter domain ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[prop-an-open-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold-has-a-canonical-restricted-smooth-structure]]).

**(a) Dust.** Let $(\rho,u,T)$ be a dust model on $U$
([[def-gr-dust-matter-model]]). Then

$$\nabla^aT_{ab}=0\ \text{on }U\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \nabla_a(\rho u^a)=0\ \text{and}\ u^a\nabla_au^b=0\ \text{on }U .$$

**(b) Perfect fluid.** Let $(\varepsilon,p,n,T)$ be a perfect-fluid model on
$U$ with comoving derivative $D$, expansion $\vartheta$, acceleration $a$ and
projection $h$ ([[def-gr-perfect-fluid-matter-model]]). Then

$$\nabla^aT_{ab}=0\ \text{on }U\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+p)\vartheta=0\quad\text{and}\quad (\varepsilon+p)a^b+h^{ba}\partial_ap=0\ \text{on }U .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and let
$U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open matter domain
([[prop-an-open-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold-has-a-canonical-restricted-smooth-structure]]).

**(a) Data.** A **perfect-fluid model** on $U$ is a triple $(\varepsilon,p,n)$
consisting of two smooth functions $\varepsilon,p:U\to\mathbb R$, the **rest
energy density** and the **pressure**, and a smooth future-directed unit
timelike vector field $n$ on $U$ with $g_p(n_p,n_p)=-1$ and
$g_p(n_p,N_p)<0$ at every $p$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). No positivity of
$\varepsilon$ or of $p$ is required or implied. A model may carry the
additional data of an **equation of state**: a function
$P:D_P\to\mathbb R$ on a subset $D_P\subseteq\mathbb R$ with
$\varepsilon(U)\subseteq D_P$, together with the relation $p=P(\varepsilon)$;
the relation is a further assumption and is not part of the basic triple.

**(b) Stress-energy tensor and derived fields.** The model's
**stress-energy tensor** is

$$T^{ab}:=(\varepsilon+p)n^an^b+p\,g^{ab},$$

a smooth symmetric contravariant $2$-tensor field ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]],
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]). The **comoving
derivative**, **expansion** and **acceleration** of $n$ are

$$D f:=n^a\partial_af\quad(f\in C^\infty(U)),\qquad \vartheta:=\nabla_an^a,\qquad a^b:=n^a\nabla_an^b ,$$

and the **rest-space projection** is the smooth tensor field

$$h^{ab}:=g^{ab}+n^an^b .$$

The physical reading of $\varepsilon$ and $p$ as a rest-frame energy density
and pressure, and their units, are fixed by the framework's matter postulate,
not by this definition.

**(c) Fluid equations.** The **perfect-fluid equations** on $U$ are

$$D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+p)\vartheta=0,\qquad (\varepsilon+p)a^b+h^{ba}\partial_ap=0 .$$

That the stress-energy tensor is divergence-free if and only if these two
equations hold is proved in
[[prop-gr-dust-and-perfect-fluid-conservation-equations]]; the definition
asserts neither divergence-freedom nor the equations.

Adopt as the field law of the direct-equation presentation of the classical
gravitational framework, for models satisfying
[[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]] and
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]], the following statement.

**(i) The equation.** Let $(M,g,N)$ be the model's smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold with metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and let
$G_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12Sg_{ab}$ be the Einstein tensor of that
connection ([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]). Let
$T$ be the model's stress-energy tensor field on its matter domain
$U\subseteq M$ ([[def-gr-stress-energy-tensor-field]]) and let
$\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ be a constant parameter with dimension
$\mathrm m^{-2}$ and $G_N>0$, $c>0$ the constants of
[[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Adopt

$$G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\frac{8\pi G_N}{c^4}\,T_{ab}\qquad\text{on }U$$

as the field law of the model. Writing
$\kappa:=8\pi G_N/c^4$ and $T_{ab}=g_{ac}g_{bd}T^{cd}$ for the lowered tensor,
the equation reads $G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab}$

**(ii) Matter content.** The equation constrains the metric and the matter of
the model jointly. A model specifies its matter sector as in
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]]: a scalar-field model with its action
and stress-energy tensor ([[def-gr-scalar-field-matter-model]]), or a dust or perfect-fluid model with prescribed
stress-energy tensor and matter equations. The consistency condition that
every solution must satisfy, $\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$, is not adopted separately; it
is a consequence of the equation and of the contracted second Bianchi identity
and is derived in [[pthm-gr-einstein-consistency-and-energy-conditions]].

**(iii) Alternative presentation.** The action formulation of the same field
law is adopted separately in [[post-gr-classical-gravitational-action]]. A
model adopts exactly one of the two presentations. They are alternative
presentations of one classical field law: the action-to-equation theorem of
this page identifies the equation obtained from stationarity of the total
action with the equation displayed in clause (i), and the direct presentation
is not an additional premise of an action-formulated model.

**(iv) Status and scope.** The equation is an adopted law of the model. It is
not derived from mathematical symmetry, from the equivalence principle, or
from observation; covariance and correspondence arguments motivate but do not
prove it. No numerical value of $c$, $G_N$ or $\Lambda$ is asserted, and no
claim is made that any particular metric or matter configuration solves the
equation or describes nature. The smooth-branch exclusions of
[[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]] and
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]] apply: distributional or
lower-dimensional sources, boundaries with junction conditions, and non-smooth
fields are outside this formulation. Comparisons of a model's predictions with
data test the combined model — geometry, matter content and this law — and
agreement is evidence about that combination, not a proof of the postulate.

Adopt one of the two presentations of the framework's field law, that is,
[[post-gr-classical-gravitational-action]] or
[[post-gr-einstein-field-law]], for a model with geometric data and matter
sector satisfying [[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]] and
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]]. Let $(M,g,N)$ be the model's smooth
time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold with metric-selected connection $\nabla$
and curvature tensors $R^{a}{}_{bcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$,
$G_{ab}$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]],
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]), let $T$ be the model's smooth
symmetric stress-energy tensor field on the matter domain
([[def-gr-stress-energy-tensor-field]]), let $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ be the
constant parameter and $\kappa=8\pi G_N/c^4$ as in
[[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Let $U\subseteq M$ be the
model's open matter domain and suppose the field law holds on $U$,

$$G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab}\qquad\text{on }U .$$

**(a) Necessary conservation.** $\nabla^aT_{ab}=0$ on $U$. Consequently a
prescribed smooth symmetric $T$ with $\nabla^aT_{ab}\neq0$ at some point cannot
satisfy the field law there with that proposed metric; the divergence is
computed using its metric-selected connection, and may change if the metric
is changed.

**(b) Trace.** On $U$, $g^{ab}T_{ab}$ satisfies
$-S+4\Lambda=\kappa\,g^{ab}T_{ab}$.

**(c) Parameter variation.** If instead $\Lambda:U\to\mathbb R$ is a smooth
function and the field law $G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\kappa T_{ab}$ holds on $U$
with that function in place of a constant, then on $U$

$$\kappa\nabla^aT_{ab}=\partial_b\Lambda .$$

Consequently, at every point where $d\Lambda\ne0$, the equation requires
$\nabla^aT_{ab}\ne0$; where $d\Lambda=0$, this identity imposes conservation.
A smooth $\Lambda$ can be locally constant but nonconstant across disconnected
components of $U$, in which case this identity does not force nonconservation.

**(d) A vacuum solution.** In the global vacuum example take
$U=M=\mathbb R^4$ with the identity chart and the flat metric
$g_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ (a smooth Lorentzian metric
with time orientation $N=\partial_0$), the field law with $T=0$ and $\Lambda=0$
holds: $G=0$ and $S=0$ for the flat metric. With $T=0$ and $\Lambda\neq0$ it
fails, since $G+\Lambda g=\Lambda g\neq0$.

**(e) Energy conditions are additional assumptions.** Neither adopted
presentation of the field law contains a clause imposing any of the weak, null,
dominant or strong energy conditions of [[def-gr-energy-conditions]]; none of
the four is a universal consequence of that equation, as the direct-equation
perfect-fluid model in the proof shows. Particular matter models may imply
energy conditions; when not derived, they are additional assumptions in the
sense of clause (iv) of [[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]].

**(f) Perfect-fluid rest-frame reading.** Let $(\varepsilon,p,n,T)$ be a
perfect-fluid model on its matter domain
([[def-gr-perfect-fluid-matter-model]]), and at any $p\in U$ let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be a $g_p$-orthonormal basis with $e_0=n_p$. Then
$T_{AB}=\operatorname{diag}(\varepsilon,p,p,p)$ in that basis, and at $p$

$$T\ \text{satisfies WEC}\Longleftrightarrow\varepsilon\ge0\ \text{and}\ \varepsilon+p\ge0,$$

$$T\ \text{satisfies NEC}\Longleftrightarrow\varepsilon+p\ge0,\qquad T\ \text{satisfies DEC}\Longleftrightarrow\varepsilon\ge|p|,$$

$$T\ \text{satisfies SEC}\Longleftrightarrow\varepsilon+3p\ge0\ \text{and}\ \varepsilon+p\ge0 .$$

In particular a model with $\varepsilon>0$ and $p=-\varepsilon$ satisfies the
NEC, WEC and DEC and violates the SEC; the inequality signs here are those of
the strict-timelike convention of [[def-gr-energy-conditions]], under which
continuity extensions to the causal cone are not assumed.

**(a) Data.** A **Friedmann-system datum** is a tuple

$$(c,G_N,\Lambda,I,k,a,\varepsilon,p)$$

consisting of positive real constants $c>0$ and $G_N>0$, a real constant
$\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$
([[def-interval]]), a real number $k$ (the **curvature parameter** of the
datum), and smooth functions $a:I\to(0,\infty)$, $\varepsilon:I\to\mathbb R$
and $p:I\to\mathbb R$, with values in the open interval of strictly positive
reals in the case of $a$
([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). We write
$\dot a,\ddot a,\dot\varepsilon$ for the derivatives of these functions of one
variable and

$$H:=\frac{\dot a}{a}:I\to\mathbb R$$

for the **Hubble parameter** of the datum ([[def-derivative]]). No relation
between $k$ and the three signs $\{-1,0,1\}$ is imposed by this definition;
the spatial model data of [[def-gr-flrw-model-data]] restrict to those signs,
and the real parameter is used so that the equations can also be examined
after a rescaling of the spatial metric.

**(b) The equations.** For a Friedmann-system datum define the following three
scalar equations on $I$:

**(F) The Friedmann equation.**

$$H(t)^2+\frac{kc^2}{a(t)^2}=\frac{8\pi G_N}{3c^2}\,\varepsilon(t)+\frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}\qquad\text{for all }t\in I;$$

**(A) The acceleration equation.**

$$\frac{\ddot a(t)}{a(t)}=-\frac{4\pi G_N}{3c^2}\bigl(\varepsilon(t)+3p(t)\bigr)+\frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}\qquad\text{for all }t\in I;$$

**(C) The continuity equation.**

$$\dot\varepsilon(t)+3H(t)\bigl(\varepsilon(t)+p(t)\bigr)=0\qquad\text{for all }t\in I .$$

We also record the **spatial-component equation**

**(S)**

$$-\frac{2a(t)\ddot a(t)+\dot a(t)^2}{c^2}-k+\Lambda a(t)^2=\frac{8\pi G_N}{c^4}\,p(t)\,a(t)^2\qquad\text{for all }t\in I .$$

Each of (F), (A), (C), (S) is an equality of real numbers at each point of
$I$; the equations involve the data of clause (a) alone. Their relation to the
curvature components of an FLRW metric, and their logical relations among one
another, are the content of the results on this page and are not asserted by
this definition. In particular, this definition adopts no equation of state:
a relation $p=P(\varepsilon)$, when used, is an additional datum.

Let $(c,G_N,\Lambda,I,k,a,\varepsilon,p)$ be a Friedmann-system datum, with the
equations (F), (A), (C), (S) as in
[[def-gr-flrw-friedmann-system]] and $H=\dot a/a$. Then:

**(a)** On the interval $I$, the pair of equations (F) and (S) holds if and
only if the pair of equations (F) and (A) holds.

**(b)** If (F) and (C) hold on $I$ and $t_0\in I$ satisfies
$H(t_0)\neq0$, then equation (A) holds at $t_0$. In particular, on any
subinterval on which $H$ has no zero, (F) and (C) imply (A).

The proof of (b) divides by $H(t_0)$; the proposition makes no claim about
points with $H(t_0)=0$, and no claim that (F) and (C) alone determine the
second derivative of $a$ there.

derivations.claim: (Stress-energy components.) In the product chart, and in the perfect-fluid sector, [L2] gives $T_{ab}=(\varepsilon+p)n_an_b+pg_{ab}$ with $n_a=g_{ab}n^b$; by [L1], $n_0=g_{00}n^0=-c^2\cdot c^{-1}=-c$ and $n_i=0$, so $T_{00}=(\varepsilon+p)c^2-pc^2=\varepsilon c^2$, $T_{0i}=0$, and $T_{ij}=0+p\,a^2\gamma_{ij}=pa^2\gamma_{ij}$. In the vacuum sector $\varepsilon=p=0$ gives the same displays with $T=0$.

(The $00$ component.) By [L3] and step 1.1, the $00$ component of the field equation reads $3(\dot a^2+kc^2)/a^2-\Lambda c^2=\frac{8\pi G_N}{c^4}\varepsilon c^2=\frac{8\pi G_N}{c^2}\varepsilon$; dividing by $3$ and rearranging gives $H^2+kc^2/a^2=\frac{8\pi G_N}{3c^2}\varepsilon+\frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}$, which is (F). The rearrangement is reversible, so the $00$ component holds exactly when (F) holds.

(The $ij$ components and the mixed components.) By [L3] and step 1.1, the $ij$ component reads $-\bigl(\frac{2a\ddot a+\dot a^2}{c^2}+k\bigr)\gamma_{ij}+\Lambda a^2\gamma_{ij}=\frac{8\pi G_N}{c^4}pa^2\gamma_{ij}$; since at each point the matrix $\gamma_{ij}$ has nonzero diagonal entries and is symmetric, this system of nine component equations holds exactly when the single scalar equation (S) of [[def-gr-flrw-friedmann-system]] holds. The mixed components hold identically: $G_{0i}=0$ by [L3] and $T_{0i}=0$ by step 1.1, so both sides vanish.

(Part (a).) Combining steps 2.1 and 2.2, the field equation holds exactly when (F) and (S) both hold; by [L6] and [[prop-gr-flrw-equation-equivalences]] clause (a), the pair (F) and (S) is equivalent to the pair (F) and (A). Hence the field equation holds exactly when (F) and (A) hold, which is claim (a), including the vacuum case treated throughout with $\varepsilon=p=0$.

(Part (b), without division by $H$.) Assume the field equation holds, so (F) and (A) hold by step 3.1. The smooth data allow the derivative calculation of [[prop-gr-flrw-equation-equivalences]] [L2]-[L3] and proof step 2.1: $\dot H=\ddot a/a-H^2$ and differentiation of (F) gives $2H(\dot H-kc^2/a^2)=(8\pi G_N/(3c^2))\dot\varepsilon$. Subtracting (F) from (A) gives $\dot H-kc^2/a^2=\ddot a/a-(H^2+kc^2/a^2)=-4\pi G_N(\varepsilon+p)/c^2$. Substituting this into the differentiated (F) and multiplying by $3c^2/(8\pi G_N)$ yields $\dot\varepsilon=-3H(\varepsilon+p)$, which is (C) throughout $I$, including every point where $H=0$. Only the positive constant $G_N$ and $c$ are divided by, so static or turning points are retained. In vacuum $\varepsilon=p=0$ the same equation is immediate. The conservation identity in [L6] also yields (C) through the fluid equations [L4]-[L5]. This proves (b).

boundaries.evidence: steps 1.1, 2.1, 2.2 and 3.1: the vacuum sector ε = p = 0, in which T = 0 and the field equation reduces to G_ab + Λg_ab = 0, is carried through every step and is part of claim (a).

step 2.1 divides only by 3 and rearranges; step 2.2 uses that γ_ij is a nonzero symmetric matrix; step 4.1 handles ε + p = 0 by the trivially satisfied second fluid equation, and ε = 0 is the vacuum case of step 1.1.

boundaries.reason: The model is four-dimensional; no one-dimensional or single-fluid-component reduction is asserted beyond the explicit component splits used in the proof.

boundaries.evidence: step 4.1: when ε + p = 0 the second fluid equation degenerates to a projected pressure condition that holds because ∂_i p = 0 and the acceleration vanishes; the continuity equation is still derived without dividing by ε + p.

boundaries.reason: Every equation holds pointwise on the matter domain U = M and the spacetime is a product with an open time interval; no boundary or endpoint value of a parameter is used.

boundaries.evidence: steps 1.1 and 2.2: the components are evaluated in one fixed product chart and the nine ij equations are reduced to a single scalar equation using the fixed matrix γ_ij; no family or covering is selected.
steps 2.1, 2.2 and 3.1: assuming the field equation, its 00 component gives (F) and its ij components give (S), hence (A) by the equivalence; this is the forward direction of claim (a).

steps 2.1, 2.2 and 3.1: conversely, (F) and (A) imply (F) and (S) by the equivalence, and the component computations then reproduce every component of the field equation, including the vanishing mixed components; this is the reverse direction of claim (a).

risk_review.notes: All five steps independently checked. Lowering n gives n0=-c and T00=epsilon c^2, Tij=p a^2 gammaij. Field-law 00 equals F; spatial equations equal S since each gamma diagonal is positive; mixed components vanish. The F,S versus F,A equivalence is reversible. Differentiating F and substituting A derives C with no division by H, so turning points and static intervals are retained. The extra fluid/Bianchi route uses the exact smooth nonempty-domain conservation suppliers but is not needed for this direct derivation. Both vacuum and fluid sectors use the same c,G_N,Lambda and exclude nonsmooth sources; no empirical premise or existence/uniqueness claim. No defect, no edit.

citations.quote:
This item assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as inherited through the Riemannian
items cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]); no further choice principle is
used.

**(a) The datum.** Let $\Sigma$ be a connected smooth three-manifold without
boundary ([[def-smooth-manifold]]) and let $\gamma$ be a Riemannian metric on
$\Sigma$ ([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]). Let
$k\in\{-1,0,1\}$. The pair $(\Sigma,\gamma)$ is a **spatial model of constant
normalized curvature $k$**, with **normalized curvature parameter** $k$, when

$$\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)=2k\,\gamma\qquad\text{at every point of }\Sigma ,$$

where $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)$ is the Ricci curvature of $\gamma$
([[def-ricci-curvature]]). We then call $(\Sigma,\gamma,k)$ a **spatial model
datum**. The signs are named for orientation only: $k=+1$ is called the
**closed** or **positively curved** case, $k=0$ the **flat** case and $k=-1$
the **open** or **negatively curved** case; no topological content is attached
to these names by this definition.

**(b) Status of the condition.** The condition in (a) is pointwise and local.
It neither asserts nor implies that $\Sigma$ is complete, compact, simply
connected or geodesically complete, and it does not determine the global
model: this definition proves no classification theorem and this page assumes
none. In dimension three the condition is equivalent to the statement that
$\gamma$ has constant sectional curvature $k$; the companion lemma on
constant-curvature three-manifolds, recorded in the Remarks, proves that
equivalence. What is used by the cosmological deductions of this page is
exactly the Ricci form displayed in (a).

**(c) Normalization and scale.** The condition (a) fixes the numerical
curvature to $k\in\{-1,0,1\}$. For a constant $\lambda>0$, put
$\gamma'=\lambda^2\gamma$. Then

$$\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma')=\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)=2k\gamma=2(k/\lambda^2)\gamma',$$

and $K_{\gamma'}=k/\lambda^2$
([[lem-gr-constant-rescaling-preserves-levi-civita-and-curvature]]).
The sign is unchanged, but for $k\ne0$ the normalized condition (a) is
preserved only when $\lambda=1$; the flat condition is preserved for every
$\lambda>0$. Conversely, if $\operatorname{Ric}(h)=2\kappa h$ for a real
constant $\kappa\ne0$, the metric $\gamma=|\kappa|h$ satisfies
$\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)=2\operatorname{sgn}(\kappa)\gamma$ by the same
Ricci invariance, so it restores the normalization. A physical model assigns
its spatial length scale through the further factor in the model postulate.

**(d) Standard models.** For each $k\in\{-1,0,1\}$ at least one complete,
connected, boundaryless, simply connected model satisfying (a) is available:

- For $k=+1$, take the round unit sphere $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$ with its
  induced metric. Its constant curvature $+1$, completeness and connected
  boundaryless Riemannian structure are supplied by
  [[prop-round-sphere-model-geometry]] with $n=3$, $R=1$ (the curvature
  calculation is also [[ex-the-round-sphere-has-positive-constant-sectional-curvature]]);
  its simple connectedness is [[thm-higher-dimensional-spheres-are-simply-connected]].
- For $k=0$, take $\mathbb R^3$ with the standard metric. Its Riemannian
  structure and vanishing curvature are [[ex-euclidean-space-has-zero-curvature]].
  It is nonempty and convex, hence simply connected by
  [[thm-convex-subsets-have-trivial-fundamental-group]], and thus connected by
  [[thm-path-connected-implies-connected]]. For completeness, the constant
  metric coefficients give zero Christoffel symbols
  ([[prop-christoffel-formula-for-the-levi-civita-connection]]); for every
  initial position $p$ and velocity $v$, the all-time curve $t\mapsto p+tv$
  solves the coordinate geodesic equation
  ([[prop-coordinate-geodesic-equation]]). Uniqueness of the maximal geodesic
  ([[thm-existence-uniqueness-and-smooth-dependence-of-geodesics]]) identifies
  it with that curve, so every maximal geodesic has domain $\mathbb R$.
  Hopf–Rinow ([[thm-hopf-rinow]]) then gives metric completeness; its
  hypotheses hold because $\mathbb R^3$ is nonempty, connected and boundaryless.
- For $k=-1$, take the upper half-space $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x^3>0\}$ with
  $y=x^3$ and metric $y^{-2}\sum_{a=1}^3dx^a\otimes dx^a$.
  Its complete, connected, boundaryless, simply connected Riemannian
  structure and constant curvature $-1$ are exactly the $n=3$, $a=1$
  instance of [[prop-half-space-model-geometry]].

By the companion lemma recorded in the Remarks, constant sectional curvature
$k$ in dimension three gives $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)=2k\gamma$, so each
model satisfies (a) and each sign is realized. A model datum restricts to one
of these global standard models only when its postulate says so.

This item assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the tangent-bundle and
manifold-product suppliers cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]); no further
choice principle is used.

**(a) Data.** Let $c>0$ be a real constant. An **FLRW model datum with
conversion constant $c$** is a tuple

$$(I,\Sigma,\gamma,k,a)$$

consisting of:

1. a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, the **time interval**
   ([[def-interval]]);
2. a spatial model datum $(\Sigma,\gamma,k)$: a connected smooth
   three-manifold $\Sigma$ without boundary, a Riemannian metric $\gamma$ on
   $\Sigma$, and a normalized curvature parameter $k\in\{-1,0,1\}$ with
   $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)=2k\gamma$
   ([[def-gr-flrw-spatial-model]], [[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]],
   [[def-smooth-manifold]]);
3. a **scale factor**: a smooth map $a:I\to(0,\infty)$, with values in the open
   interval of strictly positive reals
   ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]).

Its **spacetime** is the product manifold $M:=I\times\Sigma$ with the product
smooth structure
([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]]),
a smooth four-manifold without boundary. We write $t:M\to I$ for the first
coordinate function, the **cosmic time**, and $\dot a:=\frac{d}{dt}a$ for the
derivative of the scale factor ([[def-derivative]]).

**(b) The FLRW metric.** In product charts $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ with $x^0=t$,
where $(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ is a smooth chart of $\Sigma$, define the component functions

$$g_{00}:=-c^2,\qquad g_{0i}:=g_{i0}:=0,\qquad g_{ij}:=a(t)^2\gamma_{ij},\qquad i,j\in\{1,2,3\}.$$

These functions are smooth on the chart domain, and they define a smooth
symmetric covariant two-tensor field $g$ on $M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]): the component transformation
law is that of a symmetric $(0,2)$-tensor because the definitions agree on
chart overlaps, the time component is constant and the spatial components are
multiplied by the common smooth factor $a(t)^2$. The field $g$ is the
**FLRW metric** of the datum; we write the standard informal display
$g=-c^2\,dt^2+a(t)^2\,\gamma$, meaning the symmetric tensor $-c^2\,dt\otimes dt+a(t)^2\gamma$.
That $g$ is a Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ on $M$ and that the coordinate field $\partial_t$ is a time
orientation for it are not asserted by this definition but proved in
[[lem-gr-flrw-metric-and-comoving-data]] on this page; the same holds for the
clauses below that use the metric's causal classification.

**(c) Comoving congruence and cosmic time direction.** The **comoving
congruence** of the datum is the smooth vector field
$n:=c^{-1}\partial_t$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). By
[[lem-gr-flrw-metric-and-comoving-data]] the field $n$ is a smooth
future-directed unit timelike field, $g(n,n)=-1$, and the **comoving
observers** of the datum are its maximal integral curves; in product
coordinates the integral curve through $(t_0,x)$ is
$s\mapsto(t_0+s/c,x)$ on $c(I-t_0)$. Its proper-time parametrization is the
**comoving curve** $t\mapsto(t,x)$ on $I$, with constant spatial coordinate
$x\in\Sigma$ and velocity $U=cn=\partial_t$.

**(d) Hubble parameter and expansion.** The **Hubble parameter** of the datum
is the smooth function

$$H:=\frac{\dot a}{a}:I\to\mathbb R .$$

No field equation, no matter content, no equation of state, no measured value
and no claim about nature is part of this definition: an FLRW model datum is a
geometric object, and the physical reading of $c$, of $t$ as a clock reading,
of $n$ as the matter rest congruence and of $H$ as an expansion rate is
recorded in the physical postulates of the framework, not here.

Adopt as the geometry and matter content of a **homogeneous cosmological
model** of the classical gravitational framework, to be used together with
[[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]],
[[post-gr-field-and-matter-assumptions]] and the field law of
[[post-gr-einstein-field-law]], the following assumptions.

**(i) Spacetime geometry.** The model's spacetime is an FLRW model datum
$(I,\Sigma,\gamma,k,a)$ with the framework's conversion constant $c>0$, its
metric $g=-c^2dt^2+a(t)^2\gamma$ and its comoving congruence
$n=c^{-1}\partial_t$ ([[def-gr-flrw-model-data]],
[[lem-gr-flrw-metric-and-comoving-data]]). The spatial model
$(\Sigma,\gamma,k)$ is one of the standard complete simply connected models of
[[def-gr-flrw-spatial-model]] clause (d), with normalized curvature parameter
$k\in\{-1,0,1\}$: the round unit three-sphere for $k=+1$, Euclidean space for
$k=0$, or hyperbolic three-space for $k=-1$; by
[[lem-gr-constant-curvature-three-manifold-ricci]] each of these carries
constant sectional curvature $k$ and $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)=2k\gamma$.
The name **homogeneous and isotropic cosmological model** denotes here the
explicit standard-spatial-model FLRW ansatz just specified. Its operative
geometric assumptions are the chosen global standard model, the displayed
metric and the curvature condition; the deductions do not use an additional
undefined symmetry premise. The identification of the coordinate
$t$ with the readings of ideal comoving clocks is not part of this clause: it
is the separate clock rule of [[post-gr-ideal-clocks-and-free-fall]], applied
only where a physical clock reading is asserted. The
mathematical content used by the deductions of this page is the FLRW form
displayed above together with the curvature condition; no classification
theorem, and no transitivity statement about isometry groups, is proved or
used here.

**(ii) Matter content.** Exactly one of the following two sectors is adopted.

- **Vacuum sector.** No matter is present: the model's stress-energy tensor is
  the zero tensor, $\varepsilon=p=0$.
- **Comoving perfect-fluid sector.** The model's matter is a perfect-fluid
  model $(\varepsilon,p,n_F)$ on the matter domain $U:=M$, the model's whole
  spacetime, in the sense of [[def-gr-perfect-fluid-matter-model]]: that is,
  $U=M$ is the nonempty open domain, $\varepsilon$ and $p$ are the smooth
  rest energy density and pressure on it, and the fluid's unit timelike
  four-velocity field $n_F$ is assumed to be the comoving congruence
  $n=c^{-1}\partial_t$ of clause (i). The density and pressure are assumed
  **homogeneous**, that is, functions of cosmic time alone:
  $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(t)$ and $p=p(t)$ in the product charts, with
  values in the units of [[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]]. The
  model additionally adopts an **explicit equation of state**, one of:
  a barotropic relation $p=P(\varepsilon)$ with $P$ a smooth real function
  defined on an open interval containing the range of $\varepsilon$; or the
  constant-parameter relation $p=w\varepsilon$ with a real constant $w$ and
  the stated domain of positive $\varepsilon$. The equation of state is an
  adopted constitutive restriction, not a consequence of the field law.
  The fluid stress-energy $T_{ab}=(\varepsilon+p)n_an_b+pg_{ab}$ is the
  gravitating source in $G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=(8\pi G_N/c^4)T_{ab}$
  ([[post-gr-einstein-field-law]]). The scale factor and fluid data must
  jointly satisfy that law when a solution is claimed; the fluid is not
  treated as test matter on a separately prescribed background.

**(iii) Status, scope and exclusions.** Clauses (i) and (ii) are adopted
assumptions of the model. They are not derived from the field law, from
mathematical symmetry, or from observation; the symmetry of the ansatz
motivates but does not prove them, and no claim is made that any actual
cosmological system is exactly homogeneous, isotropic, comoving or
barotropic. The model contains no observed value: the scale factor, the
densities, the parameters $k,\Lambda,w$ and the spacetime interval are model
data, and every conclusion conditional on the model inherits the idealizations
listed in the physical scope of this item. Anisotropic stresses, heat flow and
dissipation, spatial inhomogeneities and perturbations, distributional or
lower-dimensional sources, non-smooth fields and quantum effects lie outside
the model and require additional content. Comparisons of the model's
predictions with reported observations test the combined model — geometry,
matter content, field law and the observation and analysis assumptions — and
agreement is evidence about that combination, not a proof of this postulate.

For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

For $a,b>0$ and $r,s\in\mathbb R$,
$$a^{r+s}=a^ra^s,\qquad (ab)^r=a^rb^r,\qquad (a/b)^r=a^r/b^r,\qquad (a^r)^s=a^{rs}.$$

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

**(a) Data.** A **Friedmann-system datum** is a tuple

$$(c,G_N,\Lambda,I,k,a,\varepsilon,p)$$

consisting of positive real constants $c>0$ and $G_N>0$, a real constant
$\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$
([[def-interval]]), a real number $k$ (the **curvature parameter** of the
datum), and smooth functions $a:I\to(0,\infty)$, $\varepsilon:I\to\mathbb R$
and $p:I\to\mathbb R$, with values in the open interval of strictly positive
reals in the case of $a$
([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). We write
$\dot a,\ddot a,\dot\varepsilon$ for the derivatives of these functions of one
variable and

$$H:=\frac{\dot a}{a}:I\to\mathbb R$$

for the **Hubble parameter** of the datum ([[def-derivative]]). No relation
between $k$ and the three signs $\{-1,0,1\}$ is imposed by this definition;
the spatial model data of [[def-gr-flrw-model-data]] restrict to those signs,
and the real parameter is used so that the equations can also be examined
after a rescaling of the spatial metric.

**(b) The equations.** For a Friedmann-system datum define the following three
scalar equations on $I$:

**(F) The Friedmann equation.**

$$H(t)^2+\frac{kc^2}{a(t)^2}=\frac{8\pi G_N}{3c^2}\,\varepsilon(t)+\frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}\qquad\text{for all }t\in I;$$

**(A) The acceleration equation.**

$$\frac{\ddot a(t)}{a(t)}=-\frac{4\pi G_N}{3c^2}\bigl(\varepsilon(t)+3p(t)\bigr)+\frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}\qquad\text{for all }t\in I;$$

**(C) The continuity equation.**

$$\dot\varepsilon(t)+3H(t)\bigl(\varepsilon(t)+p(t)\bigr)=0\qquad\text{for all }t\in I .$$

We also record the **spatial-component equation**

**(S)**

$$-\frac{2a(t)\ddot a(t)+\dot a(t)^2}{c^2}-k+\Lambda a(t)^2=\frac{8\pi G_N}{c^4}\,p(t)\,a(t)^2\qquad\text{for all }t\in I .$$

Each of (F), (A), (C), (S) is an equality of real numbers at each point of
$I$; the equations involve the data of clause (a) alone. Their relation to the
curvature components of an FLRW metric, and their logical relations among one
another, are the content of the results on this page and are not asserted by
this definition. In particular, this definition adopts no equation of state:
a relation $p=P(\varepsilon)$, when used, is an additional datum.

Adopt the homogeneous cosmological model of
[[post-gr-flrw-homogeneous-cosmological-model]] with an FLRW model datum
$(I,\Sigma,\gamma,k,a)$, conversion constant $c>0$, a vacuum or comoving
perfect-fluid matter sector, and the field law of
[[post-gr-einstein-field-law]] with the same $c$, the parameter
$\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ and the framework's $G_N>0$
([[def-gr-si-unit-and-coordinate-conventions]],
[[post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain]]). Write
$g$ for the FLRW metric, $G_{ab}$ for its Einstein tensor, $T_{ab}$ for the
model's stress-energy tensor and, in the matter sector, let
$\varepsilon(t),p(t)$ be the homogeneous density and pressure and
$n=c^{-1}\partial_t$ the comoving congruence. Then:

**(a)** On the spacetime, the field equation
$G_{ab}+\Lambda g_{ab}=\dfrac{8\pi G_N}{c^4}T_{ab}$ holds if and only if the
Friedmann equation (F) and the acceleration equation (A) of
[[def-gr-flrw-friedmann-system]] hold for the data
$(c,G_N,\Lambda,I,k,a,\varepsilon,p)$. Here the vacuum sector is the case
$\varepsilon=p=0$, in which $T_{ab}=0$.

**(b)** If the field equation holds, then the continuity equation (C) of
[[def-gr-flrw-friedmann-system]] holds; in the vacuum sector it holds
trivially.

No converse of (b) is asserted: the continuity equation is not claimed to
suffice for the field equation, and no existence or uniqueness of solutions of
the reduced system is asserted for any data or equation of state.

derivations.claim: (Smoothness and derivatives.) The function $a$ is smooth and strictly positive on $I$ because $t-t_0>0$, $t_*>0$, $A>0$ and a positive power of a positive number is positive; $\varepsilon$ is smooth and strictly positive on $I$. By [L2], $H=q/(t-t_0)$ and $\ddot a/a=q(q-1)/(t-t_0)^2$; by [L4], $p=w\varepsilon$ with $w>-1$, so $q=2/(3(1+w))$ is a positive real number. In particular all the data of a Friedmann-system datum are present, and $\varepsilon>0$ on $I$.

(Friedmann equation.) Since $k=0$, (F) is $H^2=\frac{8\pi G_N}{3c^2}\varepsilon$. By step 1.1, $H^2=q^2/(t-t_0)^2$, while the right-hand side is $\frac{8\pi G_N}{3c^2}\cdot\frac{3c^2q^2}{8\pi G_N(t-t_0)^2}=q^2/(t-t_0)^2$. The two sides agree identically on $I$; the cancellation of $G_N$, $c$ and the numerical constants is exact, and no choice of $A$ or $t_*$ enters (F).

(Acceleration equation.) Since $\Lambda=0$, (A) is $\frac{\ddot a}{a}=-\frac{4\pi G_N}{3c^2}(\varepsilon+3p)$. By steps 1.1 and [L4], the left-hand side is $q(q-1)/(t-t_0)^2$ and the right-hand side is $-\frac{4\pi G_N}{3c^2}(1+3w)\,\frac{3c^2q^2}{8\pi G_N(t-t_0)^2}=-\frac{(1+3w)q^2}{2(t-t_0)^2}$. The two agree exactly when $q(q-1)=-\tfrac12(1+3w)q^2$; since $q>0$, this is equivalent to $q-1=-\tfrac12(1+3w)q$, that is, to $2q-2=-(1+3w)q$, that is, to $3(1+w)q=2$, which is exactly the defining relation for $q$ by [L4]. Hence (A) holds on $I$.

(Conclusion: field equations, density scaling and continuity.) By steps 2.1 and 2.2 the datum satisfies (F) and (A) on $I$, so by [L3] and [[pthm-gr-flrw-field-equations-reduction]] the adopted field equations hold on the spacetime, which is the first part of claim (a); the special values $w=0$ and $w=\tfrac13$ give $q=\tfrac23$ and $q=\tfrac12$ by [L4], which is the rest of claim (a). For claim (b), compute $\varepsilon(t)a(t)^{3(1+w)}=\frac{3c^2q^2}{8\pi G_N}(t-t_0)^{-2}A^{3(1+w)}\bigl(\frac{t-t_0}{t_*}\bigr)^{3(1+w)q}$; by [L4], $3(1+w)q=2$, so the power of $(t-t_0)$ is $-2+2=0$ and the product equals the constant $C=A^{3(1+w)}\frac{3c^2q^2}{8\pi G_Nt_*^2}$, which is positive; the exponent of $t_*$ is $3(1+w)q=2$. Differentiating $\varepsilon=Ca^{-3(1+w)}$ with respect to $t$ and using $\dot a=Ha$ gives $\dot\varepsilon=-3(1+w)H\varepsilon=-3H(\varepsilon+p)$, which is the continuity equation (C).

boundaries.reason: The solution family is defined by explicit functions on the nonempty interval I; no empty set, empty power or empty family of solutions is quantified.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1: q > 0 and t − t_0 > 0 keep the powers (t−t_0)^{±1}, the density and all divisions defined; the dust case w = 0 is included and gives q = 2/3; no quantity inverted in steps 2.1-3.1 can vanish on I.

boundaries.reason: No one-dimensional reduction or single-solution uniqueness assertion is made; the statement verifies a two-parameter family and explicitly claims no uniqueness.
